A 100px-wide box holds at most a 10-char subtitle. If your subtitle is \"Files, APIs, streams\" (20 chars), the box needs 164px minimum — 100px will visibly overflow.\n\n**Tier packing:** Compute total width BEFORE placing. Example — 4 pub/sub consumer boxes:\n- WRONG: x=40,160,260,360 w=160 → 40-60px overlaps (4×160=640 > 480 available)\n- RIGHT: x=50,200,350,500 w=130 gap=20 → fits (4×130 + 3×20 = 580 ≤ 590 safe width; right edge at 630 ≤ 640)\nWork bottom-up for trees: size leaf tier first, parent width ≥ sum of children.\n\n**Diagrams are the hardest use case** — they have the highest failure rate due to precise coordinate math. Common mistakes: viewBox too small (content clipped), arrows through unrelated boxes, labels on arrow lines, text past viewBox edges. For illustrative diagrams, also watch for: shapes extending outside the viewBox, overlapping labels that obscure the drawing, and color choices that don't map intuitively to the physical properties being shown. Double-check coordinates before finalizing.\n\nUse SVG for diagrams. The widget automatically wraps SVG output in a card.\n\n**Pick the right diagram type.** The decision is about *intent*, not subject matter. Ask: is the user trying to *document* this, or *understand* it?\n\n**Reference diagrams** — the user wants a map they can point at. Precision matters more than feeling. Boxes, labels, arrows, containment. These are the diagrams you'd find in documentation.\n- **Flowchart** — steps in sequence, decisions branching, data transforming. Good for: approval workflows, request lifecycles, build pipelines, \"what happens when I click submit\". Trigger phrases: *\"walk me through the process\"*, *\"what are the steps\"*, *\"what's the flow\"*.\n- **Structural diagram** — things inside other things. Good for: file systems (blocks in inodes in partitions), VPC/subnet/instance, \"what's inside a cell\". Trigger phrases: *\"what's the architecture\"*, *\"how is this organised\"*, *\"where does X live\"*.\n\n**Intuition diagrams** — the user wants to *feel* how something works. The goal isn't a correct map, it's the right mental model. These should look nothing like a flowchart. The subject doesn't need a physical form — it needs a *visual metaphor*.\n- **Illustrative diagram** — draw the mechanism. Physical things get cross-sections (water heaters, engines, lungs). Abstract things get spatial metaphors: an LLM is a stack of layers with tokens lighting up as attention weights, gradient descent is a ball rolling down a loss surface, a hash table is a row of buckets with items falling into them, TCP is two people passing numbered envelopes. Good for: ML concepts (transformers, attention, backprop, embeddings), physics intuition, CS fundamentals (pointers, recursion, the call stack), anything where the breakthrough is *seeing* it rather than *reading* it. Trigger phrases: *\"how does X actually work\"*, *\"explain X\"*, *\"I don't get X\"*, *\"give me an intuition for X\"*.\n\n**Route on the verb, not the noun.** Same subject, different diagram depending on what was asked:\n\n| User says | Type | What to draw |\n|---|---|---|\n| \"how do LLMs work\" | **Illustrative** | Token row, stacked layer slabs, attention threads glowing warm between tokens. Go interactive if you can. |\n| \"transformer architecture\" | Structural | Labelled boxes: embedding, attention heads, FFN, layer norm. |\n| \"how does attention work\" | **Illustrative** | One query token, a fan of lines to every key, line opacity = weight. |\n| \"how does gradient descent work\" | **Illustrative** | Contour surface, a ball, a trail of steps. Slider for learning rate. |\n| \"what are the training steps\" | Flowchart | Forward → loss → backward → update. Boxes and arrows. |\n| \"how does TCP work\" | **Illustrative** | Two endpoints, numbered packets in flight, an ACK returning. |\n| \"TCP handshake sequence\" | Flowchart | SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Three boxes. |\n| \"explain the Krebs cycle\" / \"how does the event loop work\" | **HTML stepper** | Click through stages. Never a ring. |\n| \"how does a hash map work\" | **Illustrative** | Key falling through a funnel into one of N buckets. |\n| \"draw the database schema\" / \"show me the ERD\" | **mermaid.js** | `erDiagram` syntax. Not SVG. |\n\nThe illustrative route is the default for *\"how does X work\"* with no further qualification. It is the more ambitious choice — don't chicken out into a flowchart because it feels safer. Claude draws these well.\n\nDon't mix families in one diagram. If you need both, draw the intuition version first (build the mental model), then the reference version (fill in the precise labels) as a second tool call with prose between.\n\n**For complex topics, use multiple SVG calls** — break the explanation into a series of smaller diagrams rather than one dense diagram. Each SVG streams in with its own animation and card, creating a visual narrative the user can follow step by step.\n\n**Always add prose between diagrams** — never stack multiple SVG calls back-to-back without text. Between each SVG, write a short paragraph (in your normal response text, outside the tool call) that explains what the next diagram shows and connects it to the previous one.\n\n**Promise only what you deliver** — if your response text says \"here are three diagrams\", you must include all three tool calls. Never promise a follow-up diagram and omit it. If you can only fit one diagram, adjust your text to match. One complete diagram is better than three promised and one delivered.\n\n#### Flowchart\n\nFor sequential processes, cause-and-effect, decision trees.\n\n**Planning**: Size boxes to fit their text generously. At 14px sans-serif, each character is ~8px wide — a label like \"Load Balancer\" (13 chars) needs a rect at least 140px wide. When in doubt, make boxes wider and leave more space between them. Cramped diagrams are the most common failure mode.\n\n**Special characters are wider**: Chemical formulas (C₆H₁₂O₆), math notation (∑, ∫, √), subscripts/superscripts via <tspan> with dy/baseline-shift, and Unicode symbols all render wider than plain Latin characters. For labels containing formulas or special notation, add 30-50% extra width to your estimate. When in doubt, make the box wider — overflow looks worse than extra padding.\n\n**Spacing**: 60px minimum between boxes, 24px padding inside boxes, 12px between text and edges. Leave 10px gap between arrowheads and box edges. Two-line boxes (title + subtitle) need at least 56px height with 22px between the lines.\n\n**Vertical text placement**: Every `<text>` inside a box needs `dominant-baseline=\"central\"`, with y set to the *centre* of the slot it sits in. Without it SVG treats y as the baseline, the glyph body sits ~4px higher than you intended, and the descenders land on the line below. Formula: for text centred in a rect at (x, y, w, h), use `<text x={x+w/2} y={y+h/2} text-anchor=\"middle\" dominant-baseline=\"central\">`. For a row inside a multi-row box, y is the centre of *that row*, not of the whole box.\n\n**Layout**: Prefer single-direction flows (all top-down or all left-right). Keep diagrams simple — max 4-5 nodes per diagram. The widget is narrow (~680px) so complex layouts break.\n\n**When the prompt itself is over budget**: if the user lists 6+ components (\"draw me auth, products, orders, payments, gateway, queue\"), don't draw all of them in one pass — you'll get overlapping boxes and arrows through text, every time. Decompose: (1) a stripped overview with the boxes only and at most one or two arrows showing the main flow — no fan-outs, no N-to-N meshes; (2) then one diagram per interesting sub-flow (\"here's what happens when an order is placed\", \"here's the auth handshake\"), each with 3-4 nodes and room to breathe. Count the nouns before you draw. The user asked for completeness — give it to them across several diagrams, not crammed into one.\n\n**Cycles don't get drawn as rings.** If the last stage feeds back into the first (Krebs cycle, event loop, GC mark-and-sweep, TCP retransmit), your instinct is to place the stages around a circle. Don't. Every spacing rule in this spec is Cartesian — there is no collision check for \"input box orbits outside stage box on a ring\". You will get satellite boxes overlapping the stages they feed, labels sitting on the dashed circle, and tangential arrows that point nowhere. The ring is decoration; the loop is conveyed by the return arrow.\n\nBuild a stepper in HTML. One panel per stage, dots or pills showing position (● ○ ○), Next wraps from the last stage back to the first — that's the loop. Each panel owns its inputs and products: an event loop's pending callbacks live *inside* the Poll panel, not floating next to a box on a ring. Nothing collides because nothing shares the canvas. Only fall back to a linear SVG (stages in a row, curved `<path>` return arrow) when there's one input and one output total and no per-stage detail to show.\n\n**Feedback loops in linear flows:** Don't draw a physical arrow traversing the layout (it fights the flow direction and clips edges). Instead:\n- Small `↻` glyph + text near the cycle point: `<text>↻ returns to start</text>`\n- Or restructure the whole diagram as a circle if the cycle IS the point\n\n**Arrows:** A line from A to B must not cross any other box or label. If the direct path crosses something, route around with an L-bend: `<path d=\"M x1 y1 L x1 ymid L x2 ymid L x2 y2\"/>`. Place arrow labels in clear space, not on the midpoint.\n\nKeep all nodes the same height when they have the same content type (e.g. all single-line boxes = 44px, all two-line boxes = 56px).\n\n**Flowchart components** — use these patterns consistently:\n\n*Single-line node* (44px tall): title only. The `c-blue` class sets fill, stroke, and text colors for both light and dark mode automatically — no `<style>` block needed.\n```svg\n<g class=\"node c-blue\" onclick=\"sendPrompt('Tell me more about T-cells')\">\n  <rect x=\"100\" y=\"20\" width=\"180\" height=\"44\" rx=\"8\" stroke-width=\"0.5\"/>\n  <text class=\"th\" x=\"190\" y=\"42\" text-anchor=\"middle\" dominant-baseline=\"central\">T-cells</text>\n</g>\n```\n\n*Two-line node* (56px tall): bold title + muted subtitle.\n```svg\n<g class=\"node c-blue\" onclick=\"sendPrompt('Tell me more about dendritic cells')\">\n  <rect x=\"100\" y=\"20\" width=\"200\" height=\"56\" rx=\"8\" stroke-width=\"0.5\"/>\n  <text class=\"th\" x=\"200\" y=\"38\" text-anchor=\"middle\" dominant-baseline=\"central\">Dendritic cells</text>\n  <text class=\"ts\" x=\"200\" y=\"56\" text-anchor=\"middle\" dominant-baseline=\"central\">Detect foreign antigens</text>\n</g>\n```\n\n*Connector* (no label — meaning is clear from source + target):\n```svg\n<line x1=\"200\" y1=\"76\" x2=\"200\" y2=\"120\" class=\"arr\" marker-end=\"url(#arrow)\"/>\n```\n\n*Neutral node* (gray, for start/end/generic steps): use `class=\"box\"` for auto-themed fill/stroke, and default text classes.\n\nMake all nodes clickable by default — wrap in `<g class=\"node\" onclick=\"sendPrompt('...')\">`. The hover effect is built in.\n\n#### Structural diagram\n\nFor concepts where physical or logical containment matters — things inside other things.\n\n**When to use**: The explanation depends on *where* processes happen. Examples: how a cell works (organelles inside a cell), how a file system works (blocks inside inodes inside partitions), how a building's HVAC works (ducts inside floors inside a building), how a CPU cache hierarchy works (L1 inside core, L2 shared).\n\n**Core idea**: Large rounded rects are containers. Smaller rects inside them are regions or sub-structures. Text labels describe what happens in each region. Arrows show flow between regions or from external inputs/outputs.\n\n**Container rules**:\n- Outermost container: large rounded rect, rx=20-24, lightest fill (50 stop), 0.5px stroke (600 stop). Label at top-left inside, 14px bold.\n- Inner regions: medium rounded rects, rx=8-12, next shade fill (100-200 stop). Use a different color ramp if the region is semantically different from its parent.\n- 20px minimum padding inside every container — text and inner regions must not touch the container edges.\n- Max 2-3 nesting levels. Deeper nesting gets unreadable at 680px width.\n\n**Layout**:\n- Place inner regions side by side within the container, with 16px+ gap between them.\n- External inputs (sunlight, water, data, requests) sit outside the container with arrows pointing in.\n- External outputs sit outside with arrows pointing out.\n- Keep external labels short — one word or a short phrase. Details go in the prose between diagrams.\n\n**What goes inside regions**: Text only — the region name (14px bold) and a short description of what happens there (12px). Don't put flowchart-style boxes inside regions. Don't draw illustrations or icons inside.\n\n**Structural container example** (library branch with two side-by-side regions, an internal labeled arrow, and an external input). ViewBox 700x320, horizontal layout, color classes handle both light and dark mode — no `<style>` block:\n```svg\n<defs>\n  <marker id=\"arrow\" viewBox=\"0 0 10 10\" refX=\"8\" refY=\"5\" markerWidth=\"6\" markerHeight=\"6\" orient=\"auto-start-reverse\">\n    <path d=\"M2 1L8 5L2 9\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"context-stroke\" stroke-width=\"1.5\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"/>\n  </marker>\n</defs>\n<!-- Outer container -->\n<g class=\"c-green\">\n  <rect x=\"120\" y=\"30\" width=\"560\" height=\"260\" rx=\"20\" stroke-width=\"0.5\"/>\n  <text class=\"th\" x=\"400\" y=\"62\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Library branch</text>\n  <text class=\"ts\" x=\"400\" y=\"80\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Main floor</text>\n</g>\n<!-- Inner: Circulation desk -->\n<g class=\"c-teal\">\n  <rect x=\"150\" y=\"100\" width=\"220\" height=\"160\" rx=\"12\" stroke-width=\"0.5\"/>\n  <text class=\"th\" x=\"260\" y=\"130\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Circulation desk</text>\n  <text class=\"ts\" x=\"260\" y=\"148\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Checkouts, returns</text>\n</g>\n<!-- Inner: Reading room -->\n<g class=\"c-amber\">\n  <rect x=\"450\" y=\"100\" width=\"210\" height=\"160\" rx=\"12\" stroke-width=\"0.5\"/>\n  <text class=\"th\" x=\"555\" y=\"130\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Reading room</text>\n  <text class=\"ts\" x=\"555\" y=\"148\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Seating, reference</text>\n</g>\n<!-- Arrow between inner boxes with label -->\n<text class=\"ts\" x=\"410\" y=\"175\" text-anchor=\"middle\">Books</text>\n<line x1=\"370\" y1=\"185\" x2=\"448\" y2=\"185\" class=\"arr\" marker-end=\"url(#arrow)\"/>\n<!-- External input: New acq. — text vertically aligned with arrow -->\n<text class=\"ts\" x=\"40\" y=\"185\" text-anchor=\"middle\">New acq.</text>\n<line x1=\"75\" y1=\"185\" x2=\"118\" y2=\"185\" class=\"arr\" marker-end=\"url(#arrow)\"/>\n```\n\n**Color in structural diagrams**: Nested regions need distinct ramps — `c-{ramp}` classes resolve to fixed fill/stroke stops, so the same class on parent and child gives identical fills and flattens the hierarchy. Pick a *related* ramp for inner structures (e.g. Green for the library envelope, Teal for the circulation desk inside it) and a *contrasting* ramp for a region that does something functionally different (e.g. Amber for the reading room). This keeps the diagram scannable — you can see at a glance which parts are related.\n\n**Database schemas / ERDs — use mermaid.js, not SVG.** A schema table is a header plus N field rows plus typed columns plus crow's-foot connectors. That is a text-layout problem and hand-placing it in SVG fails the same way every time. mermaid.js `erDiagram` does layout, cardinality, and connector routing for free. ERDs only; everything else stays in SVG.\n\n```\nerDiagram\n  USERS ||--o{ POSTS : writes\n  POSTS ||--o{ COMMENTS : has\n  USERS {\n    uuid id PK\n    string email\n    timestamp created_at\n  }\n  POSTS {\n    uuid id PK\n    uuid user_id FK\n    string title\n  }\n```\n\nUse HTML for ERDs. Import and initialize in a `<script type=\"module\">`. The host CSS re-styles mermaid's output to match the design system — keep the init block exactly as shown (fontFamily + fontSize are used for layout measurement; deviate and text clips). After rendering, replace sharp-cornered entity `<path>` elements with rounded `<rect rx=\"8\">` to match the design system, and strip borders from attribute rows (only the outer container and header row keep visible borders — alternating fill colors separate the rows):\n```html\n<style>\n#erd svg.erDiagram .divider path { stroke-opacity: 0.5; }\n#erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-odd path,\n#erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-odd rect,\n#erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-even path,\n#erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-even rect { stroke: none !important; }\n</style>\n<div id=\"erd\"></div>\n<script type=\"module\">\nimport mermaid from 'https://esm.sh/mermaid@11/dist/mermaid.esm.min.mjs';\nconst dark = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches;\nawait document.fonts.ready;\nmermaid.initialize({\n  startOnLoad: false,\n  theme: 'base',\n  fontFamily: '\"Anthropic Sans\", sans-serif',\n  themeVariables: {\n    darkMode: dark,\n    fontSize: '13px',\n    fontFamily: '\"Anthropic Sans\", sans-serif',\n    lineColor: dark ? '#9c9a92' : '#73726c',\n    textColor: dark ? '#c2c0b6' : '#3d3d3a',\n  },\n});\nconst { svg } = await mermaid.render('erd-svg', `erDiagram\n  USERS ||--o{ POSTS : writes\n  POSTS ||--o{ COMMENTS : has`);\ndocument.getElementById('erd').innerHTML = svg;\n\n// Round only the outermost entity box corners (not internal row stripes)\ndocument.querySelectorAll('#erd svg.erDiagram .node').forEach(node => {\n  const firstPath = node.querySelector('path[d]');\n  if (!firstPath) return;\n  const d = firstPath.getAttribute('d');\n  const nums = d.match(/-?[\\d.]+/g)?.map(Number);\n  if (!nums || nums.length < 8) return;\n  const xs = [nums[0], nums[2], nums[4], nums[6]];\n  const ys = [nums[1], nums[3], nums[5], nums[7]];\n  const x = Math.min(...xs), y = Math.min(...ys);\n  const w = Math.max(...xs) - x, h = Math.max(...ys) - y;\n  const rect = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'rect');\n  rect.setAttribute('x', x); rect.setAttribute('y', y);\n  rect.setAttribute('width', w); rect.setAttribute('height', h);\n  rect.setAttribute('rx', '8');\n  for (const a of ['fill', 'stroke', 'stroke-width', 'class', 'style']) {\n    if (firstPath.hasAttribute(a)) rect.setAttribute(a, firstPath.getAttribute(a));\n  }\n  firstPath.replaceWith(rect);\n});\n\n// Strip borders from attribute rows (mermaid v11: .row-rect-odd / .row-rect-even)\ndocument.querySelectorAll('#erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-odd path, #erd svg.erDiagram .row-rect-even path').forEach(p => {\n  p.setAttribute('stroke', 'none');\n});\n</script>\n```\n\nWorks identically for `classDiagram` — swap the diagram source; init stays the same.\n\n#### Illustrative diagram\n\nFor building *intuition*. The subject might be physical (an engine, a lung) or completely abstract (attention, recursion, gradient descent) — what matters is that a spatial drawing conveys the mechanism better than labelled boxes would. These are the diagrams that make someone go \"oh, *that's* what it's doing.\"\n\n**Two flavours, same rules:**\n- **Physical subjects** get drawn as simplified versions of themselves. Cross-sections, cutaways, schematics. A water heater is a tank with a burner underneath. A lung is a branching tree in a cavity. You're drawing *the thing*, stylised.\n- **Abstract subjects** get drawn as *spatial metaphors*. You're inventing a shape for something that doesn't have one — but the shape should make the mechanism obvious. A transformer is a stack of horizontal slabs with a bright thread of attention connecting tokens across layers. A hash function is a funnel scattering items into a row of buckets. The call stack is literally a stack of frames growing and shrinking. Embeddings are dots clustering in space. The metaphor *is* the explanation.\n\nThis is the most ambitious diagram type and the one Claude is best at. Lean into it. Use colour for intensity (a hot attention weight glows amber, a cold one stays gray). Use repetition for scale (many small circles = many parameters).\n\n**Prefer interactive over static.** A static cross-section is a good answer; a cross-section you can *operate* is a great one. The decision rule: if the real-world system has a control, give the diagram that control. A water heater has a thermostat — so give the user a slider that shifts the hot/cold boundary, a toggle that fires the burner and animates convection currents. An LLM has input tokens — let the user click one and watch the attention weights re-fan. A cache has a hit rate — let them drag it and watch latency change. Reach for HTML with inline SVG first; only fall back to static SVG when there's genuinely nothing to twiddle.\n\n**When NOT to use**: The user is asking for a *reference*, not an *intuition*. \"What are the components of a transformer\" wants labelled boxes — that's a structural diagram. \"Walk me through our CI pipeline\" wants sequential steps — that's a flowchart. Also skip this when the metaphor would be arbitrary rather than revealing: drawing \"the cloud\" as a cloud shape or \"microservices\" as little houses doesn't teach anything about how they work. If the drawing doesn't make the *mechanism* clearer, don't draw it.\n\n**Fidelity ceiling**: These are schematics, not illustrations. Every shape should read at a glance. If a `<path>` needs more than ~6 segments to draw, simplify it. A tank is a rounded rect, not a Bézier portrait of a tank. A flame is three triangles, not a fire. Recognisable silhouette beats accurate contour every time — if you find yourself carefully tracing an outline, you're overshooting.\n\n**Core principle**: Draw the mechanism, not a diagram *about* the mechanism. Spatial arrangement carries the meaning; labels annotate. A good illustrative diagram works with the labels removed.\n\n**What changes from flowchart/structural rules**:\n\n- **Shapes are freeform.** Use `<path>`, `<ellipse>`, `<circle>`, `<polygon>`, and curved lines to represent real forms. A water tank is a tall rect with rounded bottom. A heart valve is a pair of curved paths. A circuit trace is a thin polyline. You are not limited to rounded rects.\n- **Layout follows the subject's geometry**, not a grid. If the thing is tall and narrow (a water heater, a thermometer), the diagram is tall and narrow. If it's wide and flat (a PCB, a geological cross-section), the diagram is wide. Let the subject dictate proportions within the 680px viewBox width.\n- **Color encodes intensity**, not category. For physical subjects: warm ramps (amber, coral, red) = heat/energy/pressure, cool ramps (blue, teal) = cold/calm, gray = inert structure. For abstract subjects: warm = active/high-weight/attended-to, cool or gray = dormant/low-weight/ignored. A user should be able to glance at the diagram and see *where the action is* without reading a single label.\n- **Layering and overlap are encouraged — for shapes.** Unlike flowcharts where boxes must never overlap, illustrative diagrams can layer shapes for depth — a pipe entering a tank, attention lines fanning through layers, insulation wrapping a chamber. Use z-ordering (later in source = on top) deliberately.\n- **Text is the exception — never let a stroke cross it.** The overlap permission is for shapes only. Every label needs 8px of clear air between its baseline/cap-height and the nearest stroke. Don't solve this with a background rect — solve it by *placing the text somewhere else*. Labels go in the quiet regions: above the drawing, below it, in the margin with a leader line, or in the gap between two fans of lines. If there is no quiet region, the drawing is too dense — remove something or split into two diagrams.\n- **Small shape-based indicators are allowed** when they communicate physical state. Triangles for flames. Circles for bubbles or particles. Wavy lines for steam or heat radiation. Parallel lines for vibration. These aren't decoration — they tell the user what's happening physically. Keep them simple: basic SVG primitives, not detailed illustrations.\n- **One gradient per diagram is permitted** — the only exception to the global no-gradients rule — and only to show a *continuous* physical property across a region (temperature stratification in a tank, pressure drop along a pipe, concentration in a solution). It must be a single `<linearGradient>` between exactly two stops from the same colour ramp. No radial gradients, no multi-stop fades, no gradient-as-aesthetic. If two stacked flat-fill rects communicate the same thing, do that instead.\n- **Animation is permitted for interactive HTML versions.** Use CSS `@keyframes` animating only `transform` and `opacity`. Keep loops under ~2s, and wrap every animation in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` so it's opt-out by default. Animations should show how the system *behaves* — convection current, rotation, flow — not just move for the sake of moving. No physics engines or heavy libraries.\n\nAll core rules still apply (viewBox 680px, dark mode mandatory, 14/12px text, pre-built classes, arrow marker, clickable nodes).\n\n**Label placement**:\n- Place labels *outside* the drawn object when possible, with a thin leader line (0.5px dashed, `var(--t)` stroke) pointing to the relevant part. This keeps the illustration uncluttered.\n- For large internal zones (like temperature regions in a tank), labels can sit inside if there's ample clear space — minimum 20px from any edge.\n- External labels sit in the margin area or above/below the object. **Pick one side for labels and put them all there** — at 680px wide you don't have room for a drawing *and* label columns on both sides. Reserve at least 140px of horizontal margin on the label side. Labels on the left are the ones that clip: `text-anchor=\"end\"` extends leftward from x, and with multi-line callouts it's very easy to blow past x=0 without noticing. Default to right-side labels with `text-anchor=\"start\"` unless the subject's geometry forces otherwise. Use `class=\"ts\"` (12px) for callouts, `class=\"th\"` (14px medium) for major component names.\n\n**Composition approach**:\n1. Start with the main object's silhouette — the largest shape, centered in the viewBox.\n2. Add internal structure: chambers, pipes, membranes, mechanical parts.\n3. Add external connections: pipes entering/exiting, arrows showing flow direction, labels for inputs and outputs.\n4. Add state indicators last: color fills showing temperature/pressure/concentration, small animated elements showing movement or energy.\n5. Leave generous whitespace around the object for labels — don't crowd annotations against the viewBox edges.\n\n**Static vs interactive**: Static cutaways and cross-sections work best as pure SVG. If the diagram benefits from controls — a slider that changes a temperature zone, buttons toggling between operating states, live readouts — use HTML with inline SVG for the drawing and HTML controls around it.\n\n**Illustrative diagram example** — interactive water heater cross-section with vivid physical-realism colors, animated convection currents, and controls. Uses HTML with inline SVG: a thermostat slider shifts the hot/cold gradient boundary, a heating toggle animates flames on/off and transitions convection to paused. viewBox is 680×560; tank occupies x=180..440, leaving 140px+ of right margin for labels. Smooth convection paths use `stroke-dasharray:5 5` at ~1.6s for a gentle flow feel. A warm-glow overlay on the hot zone pulses subtly when heating is on. Flame shapes use warm gradient fills and clean opacity transitions. Labels sit along the right margin with leader lines.\n```html\n<style>\n  @keyframes conv { to { stroke-dashoffset: -20; } }\n  @keyframes flicker { 0%,100%{opacity:1} 50%{opacity:.82} }\n  @keyframes glow { 0%,100%{opacity:.3} 50%{opacity:.6} }\n  .conv { stroke-dasharray:5 5; animation: conv var(--dur,1.6s) linear infinite; transition: opacity .5s; }\n  .conv.off { opacity:0; animation-play-state:paused; }\n  #flames path { transition: opacity .5s; }\n  #flames.off path { opacity:0; animation:none; }\n  #flames path:nth-child(odd)  { animation: flicker .6s ease-in-out infinite; }\n  #flames path:nth-child(even) { animation: flicker .8s ease-in-out infinite .15s; }\n  #warm-glow { animation: glow 3s ease-in-out infinite; transition: opacity .5s; }\n  #warm-glow.off { opacity:0; animation:none; }\n  .toggle-track { position:relative;width:32px;height:18px;background:var(--color-border-secondary);border-radius:9px;transition:background .2s;display:inline-block;   "description": "Creating CONTEXT.md file for the RAG trust layer thesis project",
  "path": "/mnt/user-data/outputs/CONTEXT.md",
  "file_text": "# RAG Trust and Transparency Layer — Project Context\n\n## What This Project Is\n\nA Master's thesis project that builds a **Trust and Transparency Layer** for\nRetrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. The system is demonstrated in\nmanufacturing safety but is designed as domain-agnostic middleware that can be\nadded to any RAG system in any safety-critical industry.\n\n---\n\n## The Core Problem\n\nStandard RAG systems generate answers without any mechanism to verify whether\nthose answers are actually supported by retrieved evidence. This is dangerous in\nsafety-critical domains like manufacturing, where a hallucinated answer can lead\nto incorrect or unsafe decisions.\n\nThere are four types of hallucination this project addresses:\n\n- **Intrinsic** — answer contradicts retrieved evidence\n- **Extrinsic** — answer contains claims not found in retrieved evidence\n- **Conflation** — answer mixes facts from different documents incorrectly\n- **Omission** — answer leaves out critical safety-relevant information\n\n---\n\n## What This Project Builds\n\nA pluggable **Trust Layer** that sits on top of any existing RAG pipeline. It\ntakes three inputs from the RAG system — the original query, the retrieved\nchunks, and the generated answer — and returns a structured trust report.\n\nThe Trust Layer does NOT:\n- Modify the RAG retrieval mechanism\n- Change how the LLM generates answers\n- Retrain any model\n\nIt DOES:\n- Intercept generated answers before they reach the user\n- Verify each claim against retrieved evidence\n- Score overall confidence\n- Make a decision about what to return\n- Explain why in human-readable form\n\n---\n\n## System Architecture\n\n### Standard RAG Pipeline (Baseline — not the contribution)\n\n```\nUser Query → Embed → Vector Search → Retrieve Top K Chunks → LLM → Answer\n```\n\n### Trust Layer (The Contribution)\n\n```\n[Query + Retrieved Chunks + Generated Answer]\n                ↓\n        MODULE 1: Claim Decomposer\n        Break answer into atomic verifiable claims\n                ↓\n        MODULE 2: Retrieval Coverage Check\n        Do retrieved chunks contain enough information?\n        (If not → REFUSE immediately)\n                ↓\n        MODULE 3: Multi-Mechanism Verifier\n        For each claim vs retrieved chunks:\n          - NLI Model (deberta-v3) → logical entailment\n          - Entity & Number Matching → numerical/code precision\n          - Negation Detection → conditional exceptions\n          - Semantic Similarity → topical coverage\n                ↓\n        MODULE 4: Query Coverage Check\n        Did the answer actually address what was asked?\n                ↓\n        MODULE 5: Confidence Scorer\n        Combine all signals into one trust score\n                ↓\n        MODULE 6: Decision Module\n          ANSWER    → score ≥ 0.85, fully supported\n          WARN      → score 0.60–0.84, partially supported\n          REFUSE    → score < 0.60, insufficient support\n          ESCALATE  → any contradiction found, safety critical\n                ↓\n        MODULE 7: Transparency Report Generator\n          Layer 1: Trust Score (machine readable)\n          Layer 2: Citation Trail (per claim sourcing)\n          Layer 3: Natural Language Explanation (human readable)\n                ↓\n        Final Output Returned to User\n```\n\n---\n\n## Verification Mechanisms\n\n### Why Multiple Mechanisms\n\nNLI alone fails on regulatory text because:\n- It misses numerical mismatches (500°C vs 300°C both read as similar)\n- It misses specific regulatory codes (OSHA 1910.147 vs 1910.212)\n- It often misses conditional exceptions (\"unless\", \"except when\")\n- It can be fooled by topical similarity without logical support\n\nEach mechanism targets a specific failure mode:\n\n| Mechanism | Failure Mode It Catches |\n|---|---|\n| NLI (deberta-v3) | Logical entailment failures |\n| Entity & Number Matching | Numerical and code precision errors |\n| Negation Detection | Conditional exceptions in regulatory text |\n| Semantic Similarity | Topical drift and coverage gaps |\n\n### Cascade Architecture\n\nMechanisms do not all run on every claim. Cheaper checks run first:\n\n1. Semantic similarity runs first (fast gate — if too low, skip rest)\n2. NLI runs second (if contradiction found → ESCALATE immediately)\n3. Entity matching runs only if claim contains numbers or codes\n4. Negation detection runs only if negation markers exist in evidence\n\n---\n\n## Pluggability\n\nThe Trust Layer defines a clean interface:\n\n- **Input**: query (str), retrieved\\_chunks (list), generated\\_answer (str)\n- **Output**: TrustReport (structured object with score, decision, citations,\n  explanation)\n\nAny RAG system that can provide these three inputs can use this Trust Layer\nwithout modification to its own pipeline.\n\n---\n\n## Dataset\n\n### Knowledge Base (what RAG retrieves from)\n\n- OSHA safety regulations (primary)\n  - OSHA 1910.147 — Lockout/Tagout\n  - OSHA 1910.132 — PPE requirements\n  - OSHA 1910.212 — Machine guarding\n  - OSHA 1910.119 — Process safety management\n- ISO 45001 (optional addition)\n\n### Test Queries (what questions are asked)\n\n- System requirements dataset (provided)\n- Synthetic Q&A generated from OSHA documents\n\nThe gap between system requirements language (vague, high level) and regulatory\nlanguage (specific, numerical) creates natural hallucination conditions — exactly\nwhere the Trust Layer proves its value.\n\n---\n\n## Evaluation\n\nThe system is evaluated by comparing against a standard RAG baseline\n(no trust layer) using:\n\n| Metric | What It Measures |\n|---|---|\n| Hallucination Rate | Percentage of answers with unsupported claims |\n| Groundedness Score | Degree of evidence support in returned answers |\n| Decision Accuracy | Correctness of ANSWER/WARN/REFUSE/ESCALATE decisions |\n| Coverage | Proportion of queries that receive an answer |\n\n---\n\n## Tech Stack\n\n| Component | Tool |\n|---|---|\n| RAG Pipeline | LangChain |\n| Vector Store | ChromaDB |\n| Embeddings | sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 |\n| NLI Model | cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base |\n| NER and Negation | spaCy |\n| LLM | Llama 3 or Mistral (local, open source) |\n| Evaluation | RAGAS metrics |\n\n---\n\n## Project Folder Structure\n\n```\nrag-trust-layer/\n│\n├── data/\n│   ├── raw/          ← OSHA PDFs stored here\n│   └── processed/    ← chunked text stored here\n│\n├── src/\n│   ├── rag/\n│   │   ├── loader.py      ← loads PDF documents\n│   │   ├── chunker.py     ← splits documents into chunks\n│   │   └── retriever.py   ← vector store and similarity search\n│   │\n│   ├── trust_layer/\n│   │   ├── decomposer.py  ← claim decomposition\n│   │   ├── verifier.py    ← NLI + entity + negation + semantic\n│   │   ├── scorer.py      ← confidence scoring\n│   │   ├── decision.py    ← ANSWER/WARN/REFUSE/ESCALATE logic\n│   │   └── reporter.py    ← transparency report generation\n│   │\n│   └── main.py            ← runs the full pipeline\n│\n├── notebooks/\n│   └── experiments.ipynb  ← evaluation experiments\n│\n├── tests/\n│   └── test_trust_layer.py\n│\n├── requirements.txt\n├── CONTEXT.md             ← this file\n└── .gitignore\n```\n\n---\n\n## Current Implementation Status\n\n- [x] Project folder structure created\n- [x] OSHA 1910.147 PDF downloaded into data/raw\n- [x] requirements.txt created\n- [ ] Virtual environment set up\n- [ ] Basic RAG pipeline working (loader, chunker, retriever)\n- [ ] Trust layer modules implemented\n- [ ] Evaluation framework built\n\n---\n\n## Key Research Contribution\n\nThis project contributes a **post-generation accountability system** — not a\nfix to hallucination inside the LLM, but a filter that prevents hallucinated\nanswers from reaching users. The system operates at output level, which is where\nhallucination matters most in safety-critical deployments.\n\nThe hallucination still occurs inside the LLM. This system intercepts it before\ndelivery.\n\n---\n\n## Generalisation Argument\n\nThe same framework works across industries by adjusting weights:\n\n| Industry | Most Critical Mechanism | Weight Adjustment |\n|---|---|---|\n| Manufacturing Safety | Entity/Number Matching | w_entity increased |\n| Medical | Entity/Number Matching | w_entity increased |\n| Legal | Negation Detection | w_negation increased |\n| Financial | Entity/Number Matching | w_entity increased |\n\nSame modules, same pipeline, different tuning per domain.\n\n---\n\n## Important Notes for Implementation\n\n- The RAG pipeline is infrastructure, not the contribution\n- The Trust Layer is the research contribution\n- RAGAS is used only for evaluation metrics, not as the pipeline\n- All models should run locally where possible (no API dependency)\n- The virtual environment must be activated before running anything:\n  `source venv/bin/activate`\n"
}

## User

you have suggested me to use nli with entity or number matching, negatoin detection and semantic similarity. isnt it too much are there any other ways in which we can buikd trust, one is using llm as judge.. are there any other ways?

---

## Claude

Great question — and you are right to question it. Let me give you the full honest picture.

---

**First — Is Our Current Approach Too Much?**

Honestly, for a Master's thesis — yes, it might be slightly overengineered if you try to implement all four mechanisms perfectly. But the combination is theoretically strong and well motivated. The question is really about scope management.

---

**All Possible Approaches to Building Trust in RAG**

Let me lay out every option that exists:

---

**Category 1 — Evidence Comparison Approaches**

These check whether the answer is supported by retrieved documents:

| Approach | How it works | Complexity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| NLI Model | Checks logical entailment | Medium | General claim verification |
| Semantic Similarity | Cosine distance between claim and evidence | Low | Quick coverage check |
| Entity Matching | Exact comparison of numbers and codes | Low | Numerical precision |
| Negation Detection | Finds conditional exceptions | Low | Regulatory text |
| QA Based Verification | Turns claim into question, answers from evidence | Medium | Extractive verification |

---

**Category 2 — LLM Based Approaches**

These use an LLM to reason about trustworthiness:

| Approach | How it works | Complexity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| LLM as Judge | Prompt LLM to evaluate if answer is grounded | Low to implement | General purpose |
| Chain of Verification | LLM generates verification questions then answers them | Medium | Complex reasoning |
| Self Consistency | Generate answer N times, measure variance | Medium | Uncertainty estimation |
| Reflexion | LLM reflects on its own answer and corrects | High | Iterative improvement |

---

**Category 3 — Statistical Approaches**

These use mathematical signals without needing another model:

| Approach | How it works | Complexity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token Probability | Checks how confident model was generating key tokens | Low | Open models only |
| Perplexity Scoring | Measures how surprising the answer is | Low | Detecting unusual claims |
| Retrieval Score Threshold | Only trust answers where retrieval confidence was high | Very low | Simple filtering |

---

**Category 4 — Structural Approaches**

These check the structure of the answer rather than content:

| Approach | How it works | Complexity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Citation Presence | Does answer cite a source? | Very low | Basic accountability |
| Coverage Ratio | What fraction of query aspects were addressed | Low | Completeness checking |
| Claim Count vs Evidence Count | Are there more claims than evidence chunks? | Very low | Rough balance check |

---

**Now — The Real Question For Your Thesis**

You have essentially two paths:

---

**Path A — Multi Mechanism (Current Plan)**

```
NLI + Entity Matching + Negation + Semantic Similarity
        ↓
Combined into one trust score
        ↓
Decision module
```

Strengths:
- More robust — mechanisms cover each other's weaknesses
- More novel — no single paper does exactly this combination
- Better justified — each mechanism targets a specific failure mode

Weaknesses:
- More to implement
- More to evaluate and tune
- More to explain and defend

---

**Path B — LLM as Judge (Simpler)**

```
Generated Answer + Retrieved Chunks
        ↓
LLM prompted to evaluate groundedness
        ↓
Returns score + reasoning
        ↓
Decision module
```

Strengths:
- Very simple to implement
- Surprisingly effective
- Easy to explain
- Well established in literature (G-Eval, RAGAS use this)

Weaknesses:
- Black box — hard to explain WHY it made a decision
- LLM judge can itself hallucinate
- Expensive if using API
- Less novel — RAGAS already does this

---

**Path C — Hybrid (My Updated Recommendation)**

```
Fast Semantic Similarity (gate)
        ↓
LLM as Judge (primary verifier)
        ↓
Entity Matching (safety check for numbers)
        ↓
Decision module
```

This is three mechanisms not four. You drop NLI and negation detection, replace with LLM as judge which handles both implicitly, keep entity matching for numerical safety critical values.

Why this is actually stronger for your thesis:

```
Semantic Similarity  → fast, cheap first filter
LLM as Judge         → handles complex reasoning
                        including negation and entailment
                        in one step
Entity Matching      → catches the one thing LLM
                        judges are bad at:
                        exact numerical comparison
```

---

**Why Entity Matching Stays Even With LLM Judge**

This is the key insight:

```
LLM Judge prompt:
"Is this claim supported by this evidence?"

Claim:    "Temperature limit is 500°C"
Evidence: "Temperature limit is 300°C"
        ↓
LLM Judge: "Yes, both discuss temperature limits" ← WRONG
        ↓
Entity Matching: 500 ≠ 300 → MISMATCH ← catches it
```

LLM judges are surprisingly bad at exact numerical comparison. Entity matching is your safety net specifically for this — which is critical in manufacturing.

---

**What This Means for Your Thesis Argument**

Your contribution becomes:

> *"We propose a hybrid verification approach combining semantic similarity as a fast gate, LLM-based groundedness evaluation as a primary verifier, and targeted entity matching as a precision check for numerical safety-critical values. We demonstrate that this combination outperforms single-mechanism approaches while remaining computationally feasible for real-time deployment."*

That is a clean, defensible, novel contribution.

---

**My Honest Final Recommendation**

```
For implementation:     Path C (Semantic + LLM Judge + Entity Matching)
For thesis narrative:   Frame it as a principled hybrid approach
For evaluation:         Compare all three mechanisms individually
                        then combined — that comparison IS your
                        research contribution
```

Comparing individual mechanisms against the combined approach is actually a stronger empirical contribution than just building the combined system — it proves why the combination is necessary.

**Decision 3 — Evaluation Metrics**

You need to decide exactly which metrics you report and how you compute them.

**Primary Metrics (must have):**

```
1. Hallucination Rate
   Definition: Percentage of answers containing
               at least one unsupported claim
   Compute: Human labeled ground truth vs
            system output
   Report: Baseline RAG vs Your System

2. Groundedness Score
   Definition: Average claim-level support score
               across all returned answers
   Compute: RAGAS faithfulness metric
            or your own NLI based score
   Report: Baseline vs Your System

3. Decision Accuracy
   Definition: How often did ANSWER/WARN/REFUSE/
               ESCALATE match ground truth label
   Compute: Confusion matrix
            Precision/Recall per decision class
   Report: Per class breakdown
```

**Secondary Metrics (good to have):**

```
4. Coverage
   Definition: Proportion of queries that received
               an ANSWER (not refused)
   Why: Shows you are not just refusing everything
   Report: Baseline (100% coverage, no refusals)
           vs Your System

5. Precision of REFUSE decisions
   Definition: When system refused, was it right to?
   Why: Measures false refusals
   Report: Important for usability argument

6. Verifier Agreement with Human Labels
   Definition: How often does your NLI based
               verifier agree with human judgment
   Compute: Cohen's Kappa or simple accuracy
   Why: Validates your verifier reliability
   Report: In methodology chapter
```

**Decision needed:** Will you do human evaluation or purely automated?
```
Human evaluation:
  More credible
  Required for verifier validation
  Needs at least 50-100 labeled examples
  Can be just you + one other person

Purely automated:
  Faster
  Less credible
  Fine for a first pass
  Use RAGAS as proxy for ground truth
```

---

**Decision 4 — Baseline Design**

What exactly is your baseline?

```
Option A — Vanilla RAG
Same pipeline, no trust layer
Returns raw answer always
Hallucination rate measured by human labels

Option B — RAG with RAGAS evaluation
Same pipeline
RAGAS faithfulness score computed
But no decision made — everything returned

Option C — Two baselines
Vanilla RAG (no evaluation at all)
RAG + RAGAS score (evaluation but no decision)
Your system (evaluation + decision + transparency)
```

**Recommendation:** Option C gives you the strongest comparison — you show that just having a score is not enough, you need a decision layer on top.

---

**Decision 5 — Threshold Values**

Your decision module uses thresholds:

```
Score ≥ 0.85  → ANSWER
Score 0.60-0.84 → WARN
Score 0.30-0.59 → REFUSE
Score < 0.30  → REFUSE
Any contradiction → ESCALATE
```

**Decision needed:** Are these fixed or tuned?

```
Option A — Fixed thresholds
Set them based on literature
Justify in methodology
Simple and fast

Option B — Tuned thresholds
Use a validation set to find optimal values
Plot precision/recall curves at different thresholds
Pick the point that balances coverage and accuracy
More rigorous — recommended for thesis
```

---

**Decision 6 — Scoring Formula**

How do you combine NLI, entity matching, negation, and semantic similarity into one score?

```
Option A — Weighted Average (simple)
Score = w1×NLI + w2×Entity + w3×Semantic
        × negation_modifier

Option B — Learned Weights
Train a small classifier on your labeled data
to learn optimal weights
More rigorous but needs labeled training data

Option C — Minimum Score
Score = min(NLI, Entity, Semantic)
Very conservative — flagged if any mechanism fails
Good for safety critical context
```

**Recommendation:** Start with Option A (weighted average) with fixed weights. Tuning weights empirically on a validation set is a legitimate research contribution.

| Query coverage | Not present | Did answer address the full question |
| Domain | General (finance QA demo) | Manufacturing safety — OSHA regulatory text |
| Evaluation dataset | 22 chunks, one article, 50 questions | OSHA corpus, system requirements dataset |
| Refusal mechanism | Never refuses | Refuses when evidence insufficient |
| User facing explanation | JSON confidence score | Full natural language explanation |
| Pluggability claim | General purpose | Explicitly designed as middleware |

---

**The Most Critical Difference**

This is the one that matters most for your thesis:

```
Explain-RAG:
Whole answer → NLI → entailment score → returned to user
No matter what the score is — answer always returned

Your System:
Answer → decompose into claims → verify each claim
→ combine scores → DECIDE what reaches user
→ REFUSE if unsupported
→ ESCALATE if contradiction found
→ WARN if partially supported
```

Explain-RAG is a transparency tool. Your system is a trust and safety enforcement tool. That is a fundamentally different purpose.

---

**The Second Critical Difference**

Explain-RAG applies NLI at the whole-answer level:

```
Explain-RAG:
"A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity"
vs
Retrieved chunk
→ One NLI score for whole answer
```

Your system applies NLI at the claim level:

```
Your System:
Claim 1: "Machines must be de-energized" → NLI score
Claim 2: "Workers must wear Class II PPE" → NLI score
Claim 3: "Lockout verified by second technician" → NLI score
→ Per claim verdict
→ Precise citation per claim
→ Exact identification of which part failed
```

This is significantly more granular and more useful in safety contexts — one wrong claim in a manufacturing safety answer can cause injury. Knowing exactly which claim is unsupported is critical.

---

**The Third Critical Difference — Domain**

Explain-RAG tested on a single financial article with 22 chunks and simple factual questions like "What is a balance sheet?"

Your system targets:
```
OSHA regulatory documents
→ Conditional language ("unless", "except when")
→ Numerical thresholds (300°C, 500 PSI)
→ Cross-referenced standards
→ Safety-critical consequences of wrong answers
```

These are fundamentally harder verification problems that Explain-RAG's approach does not address.

---

**What This Paper Actually Does For You**

This paper is not bad news. It is very useful for three reasons:

```
Reason 1: It validates your direction
The problem is recognized, published, real
Your committee cannot say "why does this matter"

Reason 2: It gives you a second baseline
You can compare against:
  Baseline RAG (no verification)
  Explain-RAG approach (whole answer NLI)
  Your system (claim level NLI + decision module)
Three way comparison is a stronger thesis than two way

Reason 3: It highlights your gaps clearly
Their future work section literally says:
"incorporate adaptive confidence thresholds
 to filter results"
That is exactly your decision module
You are building what they said should be built next
```

---

**How to Frame This in Your Thesis**

This is your literature review paragraph:

> *"Nadaf and Chavan (2025) propose Explain-RAG, which integrates NLI verification and source attribution into a RAG pipeline to improve transparency. However, their approach applies NLI at the whole-answer level rather than decomposing answers into atomic claims, does not implement a decision mechanism to withhold unsupported answers, and was evaluated only on general domain financial QA with a single document source. Our work extends this direction by introducing claim-level verification, a four-way decision module that controls what reaches the user, entity matching for numerical precision, negation detection for regulatory exception handling, and evaluation on safety-critical manufacturing regulatory documents where the consequences of hallucinated answers are operationally significant."*

That paragraph is honest, respectful of their work, and clearly positions your contribution.

---

**Your Contribution Is Still Valid and Clear**

```
Explain-RAG contributes:        You contribute on top:
────────────────────            ───────────────────────
Whole answer NLI                Claim level NLI
Confidence score                Decision module
Source attribution              Entity matching
General domain demo             Negation detection
                                Query coverage check
                                Manufacturing safety domain
                                Refusal and escalation mechanism
                                Natural language explanation
```

---

**One Thing You Should Do**

Add this paper to your must-read list and cite it prominently in your literature review. Then use it as your second baseline in evaluation. Comparing your system against both vanilla RAG and Explain-RAG style verification gives you a much stronger empirical story.

## User

what does empirically selected means?

---

## Claude

Great question — it is a term that appears a lot in research papers and is important to understand.

---

**What Empirically Selected Means**

Simply put:

> *"We tried different values, tested them, and picked the one that worked best."*

It means the value was not chosen from theory or a formula — it was chosen through experimentation and observation.

---

**The Example From the Paper**

The paper says:

> *"Top-k Results: k = 4 (empirically selected)"*

This means:

```
They did not have a theoretical reason
to use k = 4 specifically
        ↓
They probably tried:
k = 2 → results not comprehensive enough
k = 4 → good balance of relevance and noise
k = 6 → too many irrelevant chunks retrieved
        ↓
k = 4 gave the best results in their tests
        ↓
So they called it "empirically selected"
```

---

**Why Researchers Say This**

It is an honest way of saying:

```
"We do not have a mathematical proof
 that this is the optimal value.
 We found it works well through testing."
```

It is academically acceptable and actually preferred over pretending you had a theoretical reason when you did not.

---

**How This Applies to Your Thesis**

You will have several empirically selected values:

```
Your threshold values:
Score ≥ 0.85  → ANSWER
Score 0.60    → WARN
Score 0.30    → REFUSE

Your weights:
w1 = 0.50 for NLI
w2 = 0.30 for entity matching
w3 = 0.20 for semantic similarity

Your chunking:
chunk_size = 500
chunk_overlap = 50
```

All of these are empirically selected — you test different values on your validation set and pick the ones that give the best decision accuracy.

---

**How to Write It in Your Thesis**

```
Wrong way:
"We used a threshold of 0.85"
(gives no justification)

Right way:
"The decision threshold of 0.85 was
 empirically selected by evaluating
 system performance across threshold
 values of 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85,
 and 0.90 on a held-out validation
 set of 30 labeled examples, with
 0.85 yielding the best balance
 between coverage and precision."
```

That one sentence turns a simple number into a legitimate research decision.

---

**The Broader Meaning in Research**

There are three ways values get chosen in research:

```
1. Theoretically derived
   Based on mathematical proof or formula
   Example: learning rate in gradient descent

2. Empirically selected
   Based on experimentation and observation
   Example: k=4 in this paper, your thresholds

3. Adopted from prior work
   Using values that worked in similar papers
   Example: "following Lewis et al. we use k=5"
```

Most practical system parameters in applied NLP research are empirically selected. It is completely normal and legitimate.

---

Does this make sense? It is one of those terms that sounds more complicated than it actually is.

---

**The Honest Answer**

Giving too much detail in a cold email to researchers has a few risks:

```
Risk 1: They see you are extending their work
and feel their contribution is being minimized
→ Less likely to help

Risk 2: You reveal your exact research direction
before your thesis is complete
→ Unnecessary exposure of unpublished work

Risk 3: Long emails get skimmed or ignored
→ Short emails get read and answered
```

---

**What You Actually Need to Say**

The only things that matter in this email are:

```
1. Who you are
2. That you read their paper
3. That you found it relevant to your thesis
4. That you would like their code
5. That you will cite them
```

That is it. Nothing more needed.

## Claude

Good question — let me give you both answers clearly.

---

**Is the Paper Good?**

Honest assessment:

```
Strengths:
✓ Published in IEEE — legitimate venue
✓ Directly relevant to your topic
✓ Clear methodology — easy to understand
✓ Good baseline to compare against
✓ Confirms your research direction is valid

Weaknesses:
✗ Small scale — 22 chunks, one document
✗ Simple domain — financial QA
✗ No decision module
✗ Whole answer NLI — not claim level
✗ No real evaluation dataset
✗ Ablation study on only 50 questions
✗ Single source document — not realistic
```

It is a **good conference paper** — not a top tier venue like ACL or EMNLP, but a solid IEEE conference publication. For your purposes it is perfect — it validates your direction and is easy to clearly differentiate from.

---

**What You Are Doing on the NLI Layer**

This is the core of your thesis contribution. Let me lay out everything clearly.

---

**What Explain-RAG Does With NLI**

```
Whole answer
      ↓
One NLI check
      ↓
One label (entailment/neutral/contradiction)
One confidence score
      ↓
Always returned to user regardless of score
```

That is it. Simple, single, whole-answer verification with no action taken on the result.

---

**What You Are Doing Differently on the NLI Layer**

You are improving NLI in four distinct ways:

---

**Improvement 1 — Claim Level NLI Instead of Whole Answer**

```
Explain-RAG:
Whole answer → one NLI check
"Machines must be de-energized. Workers must
 wear PPE. Lockout verified by technician."
→ One score: 0.79 entailment

Your System:
Claim 1: "Machines must be de-energized" → 0.92 entailment
Claim 2: "Workers must wear PPE"         → 0.54 neutral
Claim 3: "Lockout verified by technician"→ 0.31 neutral
→ Per claim verdict
→ Exact identification of which claim failed
→ Precise citation per claim
```

Why this is better:
```
A safety answer can be 90% correct
but the 10% that is wrong can cause injury
Whole answer NLI misses this
Claim level NLI catches exactly what is wrong
```

---

**Improvement 2 — NLI Combined With Entity and Number Matching**

```
Explain-RAG:
NLI alone
→ Misses numerical errors
→ "500°C" vs "300°C" both read as similar
→ ENTAILMENT ← dangerously wrong

Your System:
NLI + Entity Matching
→ NLI checks logical entailment
→ Entity matching checks exact values
→ 500 ≠ 300 → MISMATCH flagged
→ Score penalized regardless of NLI result
```

Why this matters specifically for your domain:
```
OSHA documents are full of exact values
Temperature limits
Pressure thresholds
Voltage ratings
Weight capacities
Wrong numbers in manufacturing = accidents
```

---

**Improvement 3 — NLI Combined With Negation Detection**

```
Explain-RAG:
NLI alone
→ Misses conditional exceptions
→ "Lockout required unless equipment
    cannot be locked out"
→ NLI sees "lockout required" → ENTAILMENT
→ Misses the "unless" completely

Your System:
NLI + Negation Detection
→ NLI runs first
→ Negation detector finds "unless" in evidence
→ Applies modifier to NLI score
→ Flags conditional exception
→ Score reduced → WARN or REFUSE
```

Why this matters for regulatory text:
```
OSHA documents are full of conditional language
"unless", "except when", "provided that",
"only if", "shall not"
These exceptions are safety critical
Missing them can lead to incorrect procedures
```

---

**Improvement 4 — NLI Score Feeds Decision Module**

```
Explain-RAG:
NLI score computed
→ Shown to user as information
→ Answer always returned regardless
→ User must interpret the score themselves

Your System:
NLI score + entity score + negation modifier
→ Combined into trust score
→ Feeds decision module
→ ANSWER   if score ≥ 0.85
→ WARN     if score 0.60-0.84
→ REFUSE   if score < 0.60
→ ESCALATE if contradiction detected
→ System acts on the score
→ User protected from unsupported answers
```

This is the most important improvement:
```
Explain-RAG detects problems
Your system ACTS on problems

Detection without action is not enough
in safety critical manufacturing contexts
```

---

**Summary of Your NLI Improvements**

```
Dimension              Explain-RAG        Your System
─────────────────      ───────────        ───────────
Granularity            Whole answer       Claim level
Numerical precision    Not handled        Entity matching
Regulatory exceptions  Not handled        Negation detection
Action on score        None               Decision module
User protection        Score shown        Answer withheld
Explanation            Confidence score   NL explanation
                                          + citations
                                          + decision reason
```

---

**How to Frame This in Your Thesis**

In your methodology chapter write:

> *"We extend NLI-based verification in four key ways beyond existing approaches such as Explain-RAG. First, we apply NLI at the claim level rather than the whole-answer level, enabling precise identification of unsupported statements. Second, we supplement NLI with entity and numerical matching to address NLI's known weakness with exact value comparison — critical in manufacturing safety contexts where incorrect numerical thresholds carry operational risk. Third, we introduce negation detection to handle conditional exception language common in regulatory documents. Fourth, and most significantly, we treat NLI output not as an informational signal but as a decision-driving mechanism, using combined verification scores to determine whether an answer is returned, flagged, refused, or escalated for human review."*

---

Does this give you a complete and clear picture of exactly what you are contributing on the NLI layer?

    "metadata": {
      "type": "webpage_metadata",

    "is_missing": false,
    "text": "These findings underscore the need ... advancements in AI-supported engineering design processes. DesignQA is publicly available at: https://github.com/anniedoris/design_qa/. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT ......\n\nWe evaluate state-of-the-art models (at the time of writing) like GPT-4o, GPT-4, Claude-Opus, Gemini-1.0, and LLaVA-1.5 against the benchmark, and our study uncovers the existing gaps in MLLMs’ abilities to interpret complex engineering documentation. The MLLMs tested, while promising, struggle to reliably retrieve relevant rules from the Formula SAE documentation, face challenges in recognizing technical components in CAD images, and encounter difficulty in analyzing engineering drawings. These findings underscore the need for multimodal models that can better handle the multifaceted questions characteristic of design according to technical documentation. This benchmark sets a foundation for future advancements in AI-supported engineering design processes. DesignQA is publicly available at: https://github.com/anniedoris/design_qa/. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT [1], are chat-bots that can engage in conversations based on user queries.\n\nHowever, this dataset does not focus on engineering documentation. While a plethora of AI models like Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Llama family, and Anthropic’s Claude models have emerged recently, their effectiveness is almost exclusively evaluated on non-engineering benchmarks. Critical for characterizing the abilities of MLLMs for engineering design tasks are benchmarks that can rigorously quantify their performances, which serves as inspiration for DesignQA. In this section, we explore existing benchmarks for LLMs and MLLMs based on domain and reference type. See Table 1 for a concise overview. Very few benchmarks exist for engineering design problems or design requirement-related tasks. Despite the plethora of complex, multimodal QAs that could be generated from technically rich design requirement documents, very few datasets or benchmarks have been developed for this domain.\n\nPURE (PUblic REquirements) [32] is a dataset composed of 79 requirements documents scraped from the web. However, the dataset does not provide QA pairs and thus cannot be easily used for benchmarking. DesignQA harnesses the FSAE competition rules and MIT Motorsport design data to develop a benchmark of QAs pertaining to real-world design requirements. Text-based QA benchmarks that require a model to parse additional references to answer the posed question can be called “reference-dependent” benchmarks. Reference-dependent benchmarks differ from many classic reading comprehension benchmarks, like MCTest [18], which are “self-contained” and can be answered by short-text (approximately paragraph length) chunks accompanying the question. Since reference-dependent benchmarks require a model to locate the relevant information – usually across one or multiple long texts – and then apply that information to the posed question, they tend to be more complex questions.\n\nAn example of a document-grounded question, taken from QASPER, is: “[In reference to a specific NLP paper] Which neural architecture do they use as a base for their attention conflict mechanisms?” [21] As noted by Dasigi et al., document-grounded QAs tend to be more complex than open-domain QAs since they are anchored in user context and the answers are not widely available facts [21]. DesignQA, grounded in the FSAE rule document, fits within this document-grounded category. As a result, the questions posed in our benchmark are complex and rooted in user needs rather than common sense. Document-grounded questions are very characteristic of engineering design problems, as various types of documents – standards, manuals, documentation, etc. – often contain specific information that cannot be easily found on the internet. Multimodal datasets typically test an MLLM’s capacity to analyze a non-text element with respect to question text.",

Okay — I have a clear picture of this dataset now. Let me give you an honest assessment.

---

**What DesignQA Actually Is**

DesignQA is a benchmark with 1,451 question-answer pairs based on the FSAE (Formula SAE) competition rules document, developed in conjunction with the MIT Motorsport team. It has three segments — rule extraction, rule comprehension, and rule compliance — and includes questions about CAD images, component identification, and design compliance with engineering rules.

---

**The Critical Problem For Your Thesis**

This dataset has a major mismatch with what you are building:

```
DesignQA is:                    Your system needs:
────────────                    ──────────────────
Multimodal                      Text only
(images + text)                 (no images)

CAD image analysis              Regulatory text QA
component identification        safety procedure QA

FSAE competition rules          Manufacturing safety
(racing vehicle design)         (OSHA regulations)

Evaluating MLLMs                Evaluating RAG trust
on comprehension                and hallucination detection

Yes/No compliance questions     Open ended safety queries
```

---

**The Biggest Issue**

DesignQA requires models to analyze and integrate information from both visual and long-text inputs — the questions involve CAD views and engineering drawings.

Your RAG system is text-only. You cannot use image-based QA pairs for evaluating a text RAG pipeline.

---

**What IS Useful From This Dataset**

Not everything is useless. One part could work for you:

```
Rule extraction segment
        ↓
Text based questions about
what the FSAE rules say
        ↓
These are text only
No images involved
        ↓
Could be adapted as test queries
against a rules document knowledge base
```

But even this is a stretch — FSAE racing rules are very different from OSHA manufacturing safety standards in language, structure, and stakes.

---

**My Honest Recommendation**

Do not use DesignQA as your primary dataset. Here is why in one sentence:

> *It is a multimodal benchmark for evaluating LLM comprehension of racing vehicle design rules — not a text-based QA dataset for evaluating RAG trust in manufacturing safety.*

---

**What You Should Use Instead**

You already have the right answer from our earlier discussions:

```
Option 1 — Best fit (already decided):
OSHA regulatory documents as knowledge base
+ System requirements dataset as query source
+ Synthetic Q&A you generate yourself

Option 2 — If you want existing QA pairs:
Look at the text-only rule extraction
subset of DesignQA as inspiration
for how to structure your questions
but build your own pairs from OSHA docs

Option 3 — Combination:
OSHA docs as knowledge base
DesignQA rule extraction format
as a template for your question structure
Your own labeled answers as ground truth
```

---

**One Thing Worth Taking From DesignQA**

DesignQA fits within the document-grounded QA category — questions are complex and rooted in user needs rather than common sense, requiring models to locate relevant information across long texts and apply it to the question.

This framing is actually useful for your thesis. You can cite DesignQA in your literature review as evidence that document-grounded engineering QA is a recognized and challenging problem — and then argue that your work addresses a specific high-stakes subset of it (manufacturing safety) with a trust layer that existing benchmarks do not evaluate.

---

**Bottom Line**

```
Use DesignQA?    → No for your dataset
                 → Yes as a citation in literature review

Stick with?      → OSHA docs + system requirements
                   dataset + synthetic QA pairs
```

Do you want to now finalize your dataset decision and move back to implementation?

Now I have a clear picture. Let me give you an honest assessment.

---

**What the Rule Extraction Subset Actually Is**

The rule extraction segment has two subsets — Retrieval QAs and Compilation QAs. The questions do not involve images. Retrieval QAs ask the model to extract a specific rule from the FSAE competition rules document, with the format: "What does rule {rule\_number} state exactly? Answer with only the text of the rule and no other words." Compilation QAs ask the model to find all rules relevant to a specific term.

---

**Now — Honest Assessment For Your Thesis**

This is actually more interesting than I initially thought. Let me break it down:

---

**What Makes It Relevant**

```
Text only          ✓  No images involved
Rule based         ✓  Similar structure to OSHA
Document grounded  ✓  Answers must come from the document
Ground truth       ✓  Exact rule text as golden answer
Publicly available ✓  No access issues
Engineering domain ✓  Closer to manufacturing than finance
Real world rules   ✓  Actual competition rules document
```

---

**What Makes It a Problem**

```
FSAE racing rules ≠ Manufacturing safety
        ↓
Questions like:
"What does rule T.1.2 state exactly?"
        ↓
This is a RETRIEVAL task
not a SAFETY REASONING task

Your system is designed for:
"What PPE is required when operating
 a hydraulic press above 300°C?"
        ↓
This is a SAFETY REASONING task
requiring claim verification
```

---

**The Core Issue**

The rule extraction questions have a very specific format:

```
"What does rule {rule_number} state exactly?"
        ↓
Answer = exact text of that rule
        ↓
Verification = does retrieved text match the rule
        ↓
This is essentially a copy-paste task
not a reasoning or synthesis task
```

Your trust layer is designed for cases where the LLM synthesizes an answer from multiple chunks and might hallucinate. If the answer is just "extract this exact rule" — there is very little room for the kind of hallucination your system is designed to catch.

---

**However — The Compilation QAs Are More Interesting**

```
Compilation QAs:
"Find ALL rules relevant to braking systems"
        ↓
LLM must:
- Retrieve multiple chunks
- Synthesize across them
- Generate a comprehensive answer
        ↓
This is exactly where your trust layer
adds value — multiple claims, multiple
sources, potential for omission and
conflation hallucination
```

---

**My Updated Recommendation**

Use it — but selectively and in combination:

```
Use from DesignQA:              Use from your own work:
──────────────────              ───────────────────────
Compilation QAs                 OSHA documents as
from rule extraction            knowledge base
subset as TEST QUERIES
                                Your own labeled answers
FSAE rules document             as ground truth
as SECONDARY knowledge
base alongside OSHA             Synthetic safety QA pairs
                                for primary evaluation
```

This gives you a stronger thesis because:

```
You evaluate on TWO domains:
1. Manufacturing safety (OSHA) — primary
2. Engineering rules (FSAE) — secondary
        ↓
Shows your system generalizes
across different rule-based domains
        ↓
Supports your "domain agnostic" claim
with actual evidence
```

---

**What to Say in Your Thesis**

> *"We evaluate our trust layer on two rule-based engineering domains. Our primary evaluation uses OSHA manufacturing safety regulations, where hallucinated answers carry direct operational risk. As a secondary evaluation demonstrating domain generalizability, we apply our system to the DesignQA rule extraction benchmark — specifically the compilation subset — which provides ground truth answers grounded in FSAE competition rules. Performance across both domains supports our claim that the trust layer functions as domain-agnostic middleware."*

---

**Bottom Line**

```
Use rule extraction dataset?
        ↓
Compilation QAs  → YES, as secondary evaluation
Retrieval QAs    → NO, too simple for your system
        ↓
Combined with OSHA as primary dataset
→ Stronger thesis than either alone
```

    "text": "Despite the practical importance of multihop regulatory QA, the lack of high-quality benchmark datasets has hindered systematic research in this area. Similarly, existing Vietnamese healthcare QA datasets largely concentrate on clinical narratives, medical records, or healthcare-related news articles, rather than health-\n\ncare regulatory documents [19,21,15]. Crucially, none of these datasets explicitly support multihop reasoning over legally interdependent healthcare regulations. ViHERMES focuses on questions that inherently require reasoning across multiple regulatory documents, capturing diverse dependency patterns such as amendment tracing, cross-document comparison, and procedural synthesis. To construct the dataset, we propose a controlled multihop QA generation pipeline that leverages semantic clustering as a form of graph-inspired data mining to sample coherent sets of regulatory contexts, followed by LLM-based QA generation with structured evidence and reasoning annotations. ## Claude

Great question — this is actually an important distinction for your thesis.

---

**The Difference**

```
Operational HOW-TO Question:
"How do I safely operate a CNC lathe?"
        ↓
Answer comes from:
Machine manual + operator training
+ general safety practice
        ↓
Multiple valid answers possible
No single authoritative source
        ↓
Hard to verify with NLI
Hard to define one golden answer

Regulatory Grounding Question:
"What does OSHA require before
 performing maintenance on a CNC lathe?"
        ↓
Answer comes from:
Specific OSHA standard
One authoritative source
        ↓
One correct answer exists
Directly verifiable against document
        ↓
Perfect for your trust layer
```

---

**Why This Matters For Your Thesis**

Your trust layer verifies claims against retrieved evidence. For that to work properly your test questions need to have:

```
One clear correct answer
        ↓
That answer must come from
a specific retrievable document
        ↓
So you can check if the RAG
retrieved the right document
and generated the right answer
```

Operational HOW-TO questions fail this because:

```
"How do I safely operate a CNC lathe?"
        ↓
Could be answered from:
- Machine manual
- OSHA standard
- Industry best practice
- Operator training guide
- Multiple of the above combined
        ↓
Which source is the golden answer?
You cannot define one
        ↓
You cannot verify correctly
```

Regulatory grounding questions work because:

```
"What lockout procedure does
 OSHA 1910.147 require before
 CNC lathe maintenance?"
        ↓
Answer comes from exactly:
OSHA 1910.147 section d(4)
        ↓
One source, one answer
        ↓
You can verify precisely
```

---

**A Concrete Example**

```
Same topic, two different question types:

HOW-TO (bad for your thesis):
Q: "How do I change a CNC lathe tool safely?"
A: Could come from anywhere
   No single golden answer
   Cannot verify against one source

REGULATORY (good for your thesis):
Q: "What energy control procedure does OSHA
    require before changing CNC lathe tools?"
A: Must come from OSHA 1910.147
   One specific correct answer
   Directly verifiable against document
   Your trust layer can check this precisely
```

---

**What This Means For Your Dataset**

When building your Q&A pairs from OSHA letters of interpretation, make sure your questions are regulatory grounding questions not operational how-to questions.

```
Good question formats:
"What does OSHA require for..."
"According to OSHA standards, what..."
"What procedure must be followed per OSHA..."
"What are the OSHA requirements for..."

Bad question formats:
"How do I..."
"What is the best way to..."
"What should I do when..."
"How can I safely..."
```

The first set has one verifiable answer grounded in a specific document. The second set is open ended and cannot be precisely verified.

---

Does this distinction make sense? It directly affects how you design your test dataset.
