The system does not reduce hallucination inside the LLM — it\nreduces how much of it reaches the user.\n\n---\n\n## Layer 4 — The Differentiating Experiments\n\nLayer 3 produces the table. **Layer 4 produces the contribution.**\n\n### 4.1 Ablation study\n\n```\nNLI only\nNLI + entity matching\nNLI + entity + negation\nFull pipeline\n```\n\nDual purpose: this is simultaneously the strongest expected result *and* the\nbest integration test. If NLI-only scores identically to the full pipeline, the\nentity and negation modules are not actually wired in — that is a bug, not a\nfinding. Run this early.\n\n### 4.2 Numerical subset\n\nFilter to `has_numerical_answer = true`, compare D vs C.\n\nHypothesis: entity matching catches numerical mismatches (e.g. 500ms stated vs\n200ms in evidence) that an LLM judge treats as equivalent because the sentence\nstructure matches.\n\n### 4.3 Conditional subset\n\nFilter to `has_conditional_language = true`, compare D vs C.\n\nHypothesis: negation detection catches exception language (\"unless\", \"except\nwhen\", \"provided that\") that entailment-based verification overlooks.\n\n### 4.4 Threshold sensitivity sweep\n\nSweep decision thresholds: 0.70 / 0.75 / 0.80 / 0.85 / 0.90\n\nPlot **coverage against unsupported-answer delivery rate**.\n\nThis curve is a result whichever way it bends. It also converts the chosen\nthresholds from arbitrary numbers into *empirically selected* ones — meaning\nselected by experimentation and observation rather than theoretical derivation,\nwhich is standard and defensible practice for system parameters.\n\n---\n\n## Layer 5 — Error Analysis\n\nDo not skip. This chapter is often what separates a good thesis from a passing\none, and it produces material regardless of how Layer 3 turned out.\n\nTake 25–30 failures from Config D and categorise each:\n\n```\n□ retrieval failed — relevant chunk never surfaced\n□ NLI mislabelled — entailment verdict was wrong\n□ entity matcher false positive — matched page numbers,\n  figure numbers, or irrelevant digits\n□ claim decomposition error — split mid-clause, or\n  merged two distinct claims\n□ threshold miscalibration — score was reasonable but\n  fell on the wrong side of a boundary\n□ label arguably wrong — the ground truth is debatable\n```\n\nThen count the categories. If the system underperforms, this analysis explains\n*why* — and that explanation is itself a contribution.\n\n---\n\n## Recommended Execution Order\n\nNote that this is **not** the order the experiments appear in the thesis. Small\nversions of the ablation and error analysis are pulled forward because they\ndouble as debugging.\n\n```\n1. Layer 0 — label, clean, tag the dataset\n2. Freeze pipeline outputs (A comes free)\n3. Run Config D\n4. Spot-check 10–15 cases by hand → fix bugs\n5. Ablation study → confirm all mechanisms are live\n6. Run Config B (RAGAS)\n7. Run Config C (LLM judge + decision thresholds)\n8. Subset experiments (numerical, conditional)\n9. Threshold sensitivity sweep\n10. Full error analysis (25–30 cases, categorised)\n```\n\nSteps 4 and 5 exist to catch broken wiring *before* spending API money on B and\nC. Fifteen minutes of manual inspection can save a full re-run.\n\n### Dependencies\n\n```\nLayer 0.1 labelling → blocks decision accuracy (Layer 3)\nLayer 0.3 tagging   → blocks subset experiments (Layer 4)\nLayer 1 freeze      → blocks valid comparison (Layer 2)\n```\n\n---\n\n## Writing Order\n\nWrite in this order, not thesis order:\n\n| When | Chapter | Depends on results? |\n|---|---|---|\n| Now | Ch. 3 — System Design | No |\n| As you build | Ch. 4 — Implementation | No |\n| While experiments run | Ch. 2 — Related Work | No |\n| After Layers 3–5 | Ch. 5 — Results | Yes |\n| Last | Ch. 6 — Discussion & Limitations | Yes |\n| Revise existing draft | Ch. 1 — Introduction | Partially |\n\nChapters 3 and 4 do not depend on the numbers at all. Having them drafted means\na disappointing Layer 3 result costs nothing in schedule — it only changes what\nChapter 6 says.\n\n---\n\n## Positioning Against Existing Tools\n\n### RAGAS is an instrument, not a rival\n\nRAGAS operates as **offline evaluation infrastructure**: a developer runs it\nagainst a test set and obtains aggregate quality scores to inform development.\nIt cannot withhold an answer from a user. The trust layer operates at\n**inference time** on every query, and its output is a delivery decision rather\nthan a performance metric.\n\nUsing RAGAS metrics to evaluate the trust layer while positioning against RAGAS\nwould be incoherent. So: use its metrics, and position on function.\n\n**Critical caution — avoid circularity:**\n\n```\nWRONG: use RAGAS faithfulness to judge whether\n       the NLI verdict was correct\n       → one verifier grading another;\n         neither is ground truth\n\nRIGHT: ground truth = the 161 expert-validated gold\n       answers + the expected_decision labels\n       → both the trust layer AND RAGAS are scored\n         against that same ground truth\n```\n\n### Garak\n\nDifferent problem — adversarial robustness and red-teaming, run offline against\na model rather than at inference against a response. Mention briefly in Chapter\n2 to show awareness; it is not a comparison arm.\n\n### The claim to make, and the one to avoid\n\n```\nCannot defend:\n\"NLI outperforms LLM-as-judge\"\n→ likely false on general entailment;\n  a large LLM judge will often win there\n\nCan defend:\n\"A hybrid NLI + rule-based pipeline detects\n numerical and conditional-exception failures\n that LLM-judge verification misses, at lower\n cost, with interpretable per-mechanism scores,\n and feeds a delivery decision that\n evaluation-only frameworks do not provide\"\n```\n\nThe advantage is not the NLI model in isolation. It is the combination, targeted\nat the specific failure modes that matter in safety-critical technical\ndocumentation.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 2 Positioning Paragraph (draft)\n\n> RAGAS operationalises faithfulness as the proportion of claims in a generated\n> response that can be inferred from the retrieved context, computed by\n> decomposing the response into claims and assessing each against the context\n> using an LLM judge. This work adopts the same underlying construct but differs\n> in three respects. First, verification is performed using a natural language\n> inference model supplemented by rule-based mechanisms rather than an LLM judge,\n> motivated by the documented insensitivity of language models to numerical\n> discrepancies and conditional exception language in technical documentation.\n> Second, verification is performed at inference time on each query rather than\n> offline in batch. Third, and most substantively, the resulting score governs\n> response delivery rather than being reported as a descriptive metric.\n\n---\n\n## Revised Objective 4\n\nReplace the current Objective 4 in Chapter 1 with:\n\n> **Objective 4.** Evaluate the resulting system against three comparison\n> configurations — an unverified RAG baseline, a score-reporting configuration\n> representative of current evaluation-framework practice, and an LLM-judge\n> verification variant — on an expert-validated manufacturing safety benchmark,\n> measuring unsupported-answer delivery rate, groundedness, decision accuracy,\n> and coverage.\n\nThis turns the evaluation from \"I built a thing and it works\" into \"I isolated\nwhat actually causes the improvement.\"\n"

```
If NLI-only scores the same as
the full pipeline

Your entity matching and negation
detection are not actually wired in

That is a bug, not a finding
```

You want to catch that before spending API money on B and C — and before comparing a broken pipeline against baselines, which would make every number meaningless.

## Claude

Fair catch — that does look contradictory. It isn't, but only because "compete" and "compare" are doing different work. Let me separate them.

---

**What I meant by "don't compete"**

```
Don't frame your thesis as:
"My verification beats RAGAS's verification"
        ↓
Because that's a claim about which
verifier is more accurate
        ↓
And you might lose that — a large LLM judge
will often beat DeBERTa on general entailment
```

The contribution isn't "better verification." It's "verification that governs delivery."

---

**Why B is in the evaluation anyway**

Config B isn't there to be beaten on verification accuracy. It's there to prove a different point:

```
Config B = verification happens, score is computed,
           answer is delivered regardless
        ↓
This is what current practice looks like
        ↓
B vs C comparison answers:
"Does ACTING on the score matter,
 or is having the score enough?"
```

If someone asks *"why not just compute RAGAS faithfulness and show the user the number?"* — B is your answer. It shows that a score nobody acts on doesn't reduce unsupported-answer delivery, because every answer still gets delivered.

So B is a **strawman for the score-only approach**, not a rival verifier.

---

**The distinction in one line**

```
B is in your evaluation to show that
scoring without deciding is insufficient
        ↓
NOT to show that your NLI beats their LLM judge
```

---

**Where the verifier comparison actually lives**

That's C, not B:

```
C = LLM judge + your decision module
D = your NLI pipeline + your decision module
        ↓
Same decision layer in both
Only the verifier differs
        ↓
THIS is the verifier comparison
```

And even here, the honest expected result isn't "D wins overall." It's "D wins on numerical and conditional subsets, at lower cost, with interpretable output." That's the Layer 4 subset experiments.

---

**So, to be precise about what I said earlier**

I should have said: don't position your *thesis* as competing with RAGAS. Do include a score-only configuration in your *evaluation*, because it isolates the decision layer's contribution — and RAGAS is the obvious off-the-shelf way to build that configuration.

Using RAGAS as the implementation of your score-only arm is convenient. It doesn't make RAGAS your rival.

## Claude

This is the hardest question about your thesis, and it's good that you're facing it now rather than in the defense. Let me give you a real answer rather than a reassuring one.

---

**First — check the premise**

"LLM-as-judge is better" isn't established. It's better at *general entailment reasoning*. That's one axis. And you don't actually know the result yet — Config C vs D is an experiment you haven't run. Answering as though you already lost is premature.

More importantly, "better" for a safety system deployed on a shop floor is not the same as "better" on an entailment benchmark.

---

**The five axes where your layer's significance doesn't depend on winning on accuracy**

**1. Auditability**

```
LLM judge output:
"Unsupported." — and a score
        ↓
Why? Unrecoverable. The reasoning
is inside a model you can't inspect.

Your pipeline output:
NLI: NEUTRAL (0.51)
Entity: MISMATCH — claim "500ms",
        evidence "200ms"
Negation: "unless" detected in evidence
Semantic: 0.61
→ combined 0.44 → REFUSE
        ↓
Every component of the decision is visible
and attributable to a specific mechanism
```

In a setting where an injury might trigger an inquiry into why the system said what it said, "the LLM judged it unsupported" is a materially weaker answer than a decomposable score.

**2. Correlated failure**

This is the argument I think is strongest and I haven't raised it yet.

```
Generator: an LLM
Judge:     an LLM
        ↓
If they share training data, architecture,
or failure modes, they may share blind spots
        ↓
The judge may confidently approve exactly
the fabrications the generator is prone to
```

DeBERTa is a different architecture trained on a different objective. Entity matching is not a neural model at all. Architectural diversity in a verification chain is a real engineering principle, not a rationalization.

**3. Determinism and reproducibility**

```
Your pipeline: fixed weights, fixed thresholds
→ same input, same output, indefinitely
→ reproducible by anyone, forever

LLM judge: API model versions deprecate
→ gpt-4o-mini today ≠ gpt-4o-mini in 18 months
→ your published results become unreproducible
```

For a thesis that claims to be a *safety* component, a verifier whose behavior can change under you without notice is a genuine liability.

**4. Data locality**

Manufacturing firms frequently cannot send operational data to external APIs — proprietary process parameters, equipment configurations, sometimes contractual restrictions. A verification layer that requires an API call per claim is undeployable in those environments. Yours runs entirely local.

**5. Targeted hardening**

Entity matching and negation detection exist because entailment models — LLM judges included — are documented to be weak on exactly the two things that kill people in procedural documentation: wrong numbers and missed exceptions. That's not a general accuracy claim. It's a claim about specific failure modes, and it's testable in your Layer 4 subset experiments.

---

**Answering "why NLI and not LLM-as-judge"**

> We deliberately avoided LLM-as-judge verification for three reasons. First, auditability: a verification decision in a safety-critical setting should be decomposable into inspectable components rather than delegated to an opaque model. Second, correlated failure: using a language model to verify a language model risks shared blind spots, whereas an NLI model supplemented by rule-based checks provides architectural diversity in the verification chain. Third, deployability: local inference imposes no per-query cost and requires no transmission of operational data to external services, which is a hard constraint in many manufacturing environments. We include an LLM-judge configuration in our evaluation precisely so this design choice can be assessed empirically rather than assumed.

That last sentence is the important one. You didn't avoid LLM-judge out of ignorance — you tested it.

---

**Answering "why not just use RAGAS faithfulness"**

> RAGAS faithfulness is an offline evaluation metric. It produces an aggregate score to inform system development; it does not operate at inference time and it cannot withhold a response from a user. Substituting it for the proposed verification layer would supply a number but not a decision, no per-claim source attribution, and no explanation — and every answer, including unsupported ones, would still be delivered. We use RAGAS in this work, but as a comparison configuration and as a source of standard metrics, not as a replacement for the layer.

The one-line version if pressed in a defense: **RAGAS tells the developer how the system performed. My layer tells the operator whether to act on this answer.**

---

**The point that makes all of this robust**

Your contribution is the *layer* — decompose, verify, score, decide, explain. The verification mechanism is a **pluggable component inside it.**

```
If C beats D:
Your layer still stands
You swap the mechanism
        ↓
Finding: "the decision layer drives most of
the improvement; verifier choice is a
cost/auditability tradeoff rather than an
accuracy one"
        ↓
That is a useful, publishable result
```

You designed the architecture to be mechanism-agnostic. That means "which verifier is best" is an empirical question you answer *within* your framework — not a threat to the framework itself.

The thesis question was never "is DeBERTa better than GPT." It's "does verification-gated delivery reduce unsupported answers reaching users, and what are the tradeoffs among verification mechanisms." Both halves of that get answered regardless of which way C vs D falls.

    "text": "## 2.3 Evaluation Metrics\n\nWe report: AUROC and AUPRC for hallucination detection, and Excess Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (E-AURC) and Target Calibration Error (TCE) to evaluate selective prediction.\n\n**E-AURC.** We form a risk–coverage (RC) curve by sorting examples by the risk score and, for each acceptance threshold, measuring (a) *coverage*, the fraction of examples answered, and (b) *selective risk*, the hallucination rate among answered examples. AURC is the area under this RC curve. E-AURC is the excess area relative to an oracle ranking that abstains on all hallucinations before abstaining on any correct examples, providing a unitless measure in [0, 1] (Geifman et al., 2019).\n\n**TCE.** For calibration, we sweep target risks $\\alpha$ over an operational range $\\mathcal{A}$ and measure how closely the calibrated policy achieves each target on the test set:\n\n$$TCE = \\mathbb{E}_{\\alpha \\sim \\mathcal{A}} [|R_{\\text{test}}(\\alpha) - \\alpha|].$$\n\n\n\nwhere $R_{\\text{test}}(\\alpha)$ is the test set selective risk when the acceptance threshold is tuned to target $\\alpha$ .\n\nWe use TCE rather than standard calibration metrics such as ECE because our goal is accurate risk control at *specific operating points*, rather than global probability calibration over [0, 1].",

This is the single most important question anyone will ask you, and Dr. Maier is right to push on it. There's an established answer — this exact problem has a literature, and it's the "who verifies the verifier" problem.

Let me separate what he's probably asking, because there are two distinct questions hiding in it.

---

**Reading 1: "Why those weights and thresholds?"**

Right now your score is `0.50×NLI + 0.30×entity + 0.20×semantic`, thresholds at 0.85/0.60/0.30, negation modifier of 0.5. Every one of those numbers is currently arbitrary. A score of 0.548 has no external meaning.

**Reading 2: "How do you know your verifier's judgments are correct?"**

Your NLI says NEUTRAL. Says who? What makes that the right label?

Both need answering, and the answers are different.

---

**The reframe that fixes most of this**

Your composite score is an *intermediate artifact*. It has no external referent, so validating "is 0.548 correct?" is meaningless. What has an external referent is:

```
Per-claim: is this claim actually supported
           by the evidence? (human judgment)

Per-answer: was ANSWER/WARN/REFUSE/ESCALATE
            the right decision? (your labels)
```

Validate those. The score is just the mechanism that gets you there.

---

**Three levels of validation, all with precedent**

**Level 1 — Component validation (free, do today)**

DeBERTa-v3's NLI performance on MNLI and ANLI is published. Report those benchmark numbers in Chapter 4. You didn't invent the entailment model; its accuracy is established independently of your work. Same for your embedding model on STS benchmarks.

This answers: *is the NLI component a reasonable instrument?* Answer: here are its published numbers.

**Level 2 — Verifier validation against human labels**

This is the core of what Maier wants, and there's a clear established methodology.

SummaC uses balanced accuracy as the primary evaluation metric, chosen because accuracy is conceptually simple and interpretable, and adjusting class imbalance out of the metric makes scores more uniform across datasets, with ROC-AUC as secondary.

TRUE goes further on a point that matters for you: it argues that system-level correlation with human judgment is the wrong meta-evaluation target, and instead recasts annotated datasets into a single binary labelling scheme scored by example-level ROC AUC.

So the procedure is:

```
1. Sample ~150-200 claims from your pipeline output
2. Hand-label each: supported / not supported
   (you + ideally one other annotator)
3. Compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ)
4. Score your verifier against those labels:
   → balanced accuracy (primary)
   → ROC-AUC (secondary)
   → per-class precision/recall
```

Now when Maier asks "on what basis," the answer is: *"My verifier agrees with human judgment at X balanced accuracy and Y ROC-AUC, measured on Z independently-labeled claims, using the meta-evaluation protocol established by SummaC and TRUE."*

That is a citable, defensible basis.

**Level 3 — Decision validation via risk-coverage**

This is where your four-way decision module gets validated, and it's the piece I think will most impress him because it's the established framework for exactly what you built.

Allowing a classifier to abstain and measuring the coverage–risk tradeoff is a classical framework (El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017). The two quantities:

```
Coverage = fraction of questions you answer
Selective risk = error rate among answered questions
```

One paper states the deployment logic explicitly: because the motivating use case is abstention, the key deployment metric is not AUROC alone but selective prediction behavior.

So you report a **risk-coverage curve**: sweep your threshold, plot coverage against unsupported-answer rate. Then report operating points — *"at 80% coverage, unsupported delivery drops from 0.31 to 0.09."* That single sentence is worth more than any composite score.

And the area under that curve (AURC, or E-AURC against an oracle) gives you a single summary number with actual meaning.

---

**How thresholds stop being arbitrary**

You need a split. Non-negotiable.

```
161 questions
        ↓
Validation set (~50)  → select weights and thresholds here
Test set (~111)       → report results here, touch once
```

SummaC does exactly this: the threshold is selected using the validation set, allowing for a different threshold for each dataset in the benchmark.

If you tune thresholds and report on the same 161 questions, Maier can dismiss every number as overfit — and he'd be right. Split now, before you run anything.

The selective-prediction framing gives you something even better. Instead of picking 0.85 because it feels right, you can pick it to *hit a risk target*: choose the threshold that maximizes coverage subject to selective risk staying below some tolerance on the validation set. That converts your threshold from a guess into a decision derived from a stated safety requirement — which for a manufacturing safety thesis is a much stronger story.

---

**How weights stop being arbitrary**

Three options, increasing in rigor:

```
Option A — Grid search on validation set
Sweep w1/w2/w3 combinations, pick best
balanced accuracy. Report the search.

Option B — Ablations do the work instead
Report NLI-only, +entity, +negation, full.
If each addition improves things, the
weights matter less than the components.

Option C — Learn them
Fit logistic regression on validation labels
with the three component scores as features.
Weights become fitted coefficients.
```

Option B is what I'd recommend given your timeline. Option C is the most defensible and is genuinely not much work — it's three features and ~50 labeled examples.

---

**Two additions that will specifically satisfy him**

**Statistical significance.** SummaC tests improvements via bootstrap resampling, comparing models to the best-performing prior model, with Bonferroni correction applied across multiple tests. With 161 questions your confidence intervals will be wide — better to show them than to have him ask.

**Calibration.** Does a score of 0.85 actually mean 85% likely supported? Bin your scores, compare average predicted confidence to empirical correctness per bin, compute expected calibration error:

```
ECE = Σ (n_b/n) × |accuracy(b) − confidence(b)|
```

A reliability diagram showing your scores are roughly calibrated is direct evidence that the numbers mean something. If they're badly calibrated, that's a finding too — and temperature scaling can fix it without changing any labels.

---

**What to actually say to Dr. Maier**

> The composite score is an internal mechanism, not a claim about the world, so I validate the outputs it produces rather than the score itself. Verification is validated against human-labeled claim support using balanced accuracy and ROC-AUC, following the meta-evaluation protocol of SummaC and TRUE. Decision quality is validated through risk-coverage analysis from the selective prediction literature, reporting selective risk at fixed coverage levels. Weights and thresholds are selected on a held-out validation split and never on the test set, and I report calibration error to show the scores are meaningful rather than merely ordinal.

---

**The one thing to do before your next meeting with him**

Split your 161 questions into validation and test, and hand-label 100–150 individual claims for support. Everything above depends on having human labels; without them you have no ground truth for the verifier and no honest answer to his question.

Want me to add this as a validation section in your `EVALUATION_PLAN.md`? It changes the plan materially — the data split and the claim-labeling task are new prerequisites that belong in Layer 0.

---

## Claude

Two honest answers.

---

**Can you be the labeler?**

Yes. With conditions.

You are labeling *"is this claim supported by this text?"* — not *"is this safe manufacturing practice?"* The first is a reading-comprehension judgment. The second would need a safety engineer. You only need the first.

```
What you're judging:
Claim:    "The arm stops within 500ms"
Evidence: "...stopping time 200ms..."
        ↓
Is the claim supported? No.
        ↓
No manufacturing expertise required
```

What makes single-annotator labeling defensible:

```
1. Write a labeling protocol BEFORE you start
   Define supported / not supported / unclear
   Write down the edge-case rules
   → this becomes a thesis appendix

2. Get a second annotator on a subset
   ~30-40 claims, compute Cohen's κ
   Another grad student works fine
   κ above ~0.6 is respectable

3. Have Dr. Morkos review 15-20
   Not to relabel everything — just to
   confirm your protocol is sound

4. Declare it in your limitations
   "Labels produced by the author following
    a documented protocol; agreement
    validated on a subset"
```

Single-annotator datasets appear in published work constantly. What's not defensible is undocumented labeling with no agreement check.

One note: your gold answers are already expert-validated by Megahed's team. So for the *decision* labels, you're often reasoning from expert-written answers rather than from scratch. That's a meaningful backstop.

---

**Is all of it necessary?**

No. I gave you the full menu; here's the triage.

**Necessary — Maier's question fails without these**

```
□ Validation/test split
  Zero extra work. Just split the file.
  Without it, every number is overfit.

□ expected_decision labels on all 161
  Already in your plan. This is your
  decision-accuracy ground truth.

□ Risk-coverage curve
  Threshold sweep you'd already planned,
  plotted as coverage vs unsupported rate.
  This is THE answer to "on what basis" —
  it makes your thresholds derived rather
  than guessed.

□ Claim-level labels, but only ~60-80
  Not 150. Enough for balanced accuracy
  with wide-but-honest confidence intervals.
  A few hours.
```

**Worth doing — meaningfully strengthens it**

```
□ Cohen's κ on a 30-claim subset
□ Component benchmark numbers in Ch. 4
  (published DeBERTa MNLI figures —
   pure citation, no work)
□ Ablations
  Already planned. Do these instead of
  grid-searching weights.
```

**Skip unless time allows**

```
□ ECE and reliability diagrams
□ Bootstrap significance testing
□ Learned weights via logistic regression
□ Full 150+ claim labeling
```

That bottom group is what a PhD would do. Fine as future work.

---

**The minimum that answers him**

```
1. Split the data
2. Label ~70 claims with a written protocol
3. Report balanced accuracy + ROC-AUC
4. Report the risk-coverage curve
5. Label expected_decision on all 161
```

Roughly a day of focused work, most of which was already on your plan. Steps 1 and 4 are nearly free and do the heaviest lifting.

---

**One reframe worth holding onto**

Maier didn't ask you to build a validation apparatus. He asked *on what basis* your numbers mean anything. The shortest honest answer is:

> My thresholds are selected on held-out validation data to meet a stated risk target, and my verifier's agreement with human judgment is measured directly rather than assumed.

Everything above exists to let you say that sentence truthfully. Anything beyond it is optional polish.

Want me to add the triaged version — necessary/worth-doing/skip — to your evaluation plan? I'd rather add the triage than the full menu, so you're not looking at a wall of requirements when you open the file next month.

Two things came out of this, and one of them is important enough that you need to know it today rather than at your defense.

---

**First — the good news: your methodology has solid precedent**

You are not inventing evaluation methodology. The field has converged on exactly what I described:

**SABER — "Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach"** (arXiv:2605.18792) reports a full threshold sweep over τ from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, reporting Score, Coverage, Risk on answered, and abstention F1.

That is your threshold sweep, with the exact metrics I suggested. You can cite it as methodological precedent.

**Citation-Enforced RAG for tax compliance** (arXiv:2603.14170) grounds abstention in retrieval confidence, noting that basing abstention on retrieval behaviour rather than generative uncertainty alone ties decisions directly to evidence availability — that's your Retrieval Coverage Check, justified.

**Prompt-Based Abstention Fails Under Misleading Context** (arXiv:2608.22228) says something useful for your positioning: abstention is well-studied in selective prediction, but for RAG most work either folds it into broader system evaluation or targets frontier models.

So: your methodology is defensible and citable. Dr. Maier's question has established answers.

---

**Second — and you need to read this carefully**

There is a paper very close to your architecture:

**"Claim-Selective Certification for High-Risk Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation"** (arXiv:2605.21949)

They describe claim-selective certification as decomposing a question into verifiable claim units, scoring each claim against evidence, and choosing whether to state it directly, state it with conditions, contest it, or withhold it.

```
Their four actions:        Your four decisions:
────────────────────       ───────────────────
state directly         ≈   ANSWER
state with conditions  ≈   WARN
contest                ≈   ESCALATE
withhold               ≈   REFUSE
```

Their implementation has three stages: template-based claim decomposition, cue-based relation scoring for support/conflict/limitation signals, and an intent-aware risk-calibrated selector.

They also motivate it the way you do — that high-risk medical QA has an asymmetric answer contract, where unsupported dosing or contraindication claims can be harmful while blanket abstention suppresses usable evidence.

I'm not going to soften this. Claim decomposition plus per-claim evidence scoring plus four-way action selection in a safety-critical domain has been published.

---

**What is genuinely still yours**

Three real differences, and one of them is substantial.

**1. Pipeline position — this is the big one.** Their own paper states that claim-selective RAG uses the signal earlier in the pipeline, before the final response is formed, mapping each claim to an action rather than only scoring a completed answer.

```
Them: intervene DURING response construction
      per-claim actions assembled into an answer

You:  intervene AFTER generation
      answer-level decision on a completed answer
      → true post-hoc middleware
      → works on any RAG without touching it
```

Your pluggability claim survives this cleanly. Theirs requires integration into generation; yours does not.

**2. Verification mechanism.** They use "cue-based relation scoring." You use NLI plus entity matching plus negation detection. Different instruments.

**3. Domain.** Medical versus manufacturing. Weaker as a differentiator, but real — and your regulatory/OEM document mix is distinctive.

---

**What to do about it**

```
1. Read arXiv:2605.21949 in full, this week
2. It becomes your primary related work —
   ahead of Explain-RAG
```

## Claude

Your instinct is exactly right, and it's worth stating plainly: **established methodology is a strength, not a weakness.** Let me take both questions.

---

**What "shift the framing" means concretely**

Right now your framing leads with the decision module. That's the part that now has close prior work. So lead with what doesn't.

```
Current framing:
"A four-way decision module for RAG"
        ↓
Claim-selective certification does this

Shifted framing:
"Post-hoc middleware that adds verification-gated
 delivery to an unmodified RAG pipeline"
        ↓
Theirs integrates into generation.
Yours requires nothing from the host system.
```

The practical difference matters and you can state it sharply: their approach requires access to the generation process. Yours requires three strings — query, chunks, answer. Any deployed RAG system can adopt yours tomorrow without being rebuilt.

That's the property to put in your title and abstract. The decision module becomes *how* the middleware works, not the headline claim.

---

**On novelty vs. methodology**

You've identified something real. These are two different things and they have opposite requirements:

```
Contribution → should be novel
               (your middleware, your hybrid verifier,
                your domain, your comparative evaluation)

Methodology  → should be ESTABLISHED
               (balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC,
                risk-coverage curves)
```

Inventing your own evaluation metric would be a liability. "I made up a metric and my system scores well on it" is exactly what Maier was pushing back against. Using SummaC's and SABER's protocols means the numbers mean something independent of you.

So: prior work on *methodology* is load-bearing support. Prior work on *contribution* is what you differentiate from. Different roles.

---

**Now the useful part — can you use these papers instead of SummaC?**

Partly yes, and it saves you real work. But they validate different things:

```
SummaC / TRUE
→ validates the VERIFIER
→ "does my NLI agree with human judgment?"
→ needs: claim-level human labels (~70)
→ metrics: balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC

SABER / selective prediction
→ validates the DECISION LAYER
→ "does abstaining actually reduce risk?"
→ needs: expected_decision labels (already planned)
→ metrics: coverage, risk-on-answered, abstention F1
```

Here's the scoping argument worth considering:

**Your contribution is the decision layer, not the verifier.** You didn't build DeBERTa. So you could legitimately validate at the decision level only, and cite DeBERTa's published MNLI numbers for the component.

```
If time is tight:
□ SABER-style decision validation
  (coverage, risk, abstention F1, threshold sweep)
  → uses labels you're already making
□ Cite published DeBERTa benchmark numbers
  → zero work
□ SKIP the 70 claim-level labels
```

That drops the claim-labeling task entirely. The defense line becomes:

> Verifier component performance is established in prior work; this thesis validates the decision layer, which is its contribution, using the selective-prediction protocol.

That's honest and defensible.

**But** — if you can manage 50-70 claim labels, do it. It lets you say something the decision-level analysis can't: that your *hybrid* verifier outperforms NLI alone on numerical and conditional claims. That's your Layer 4 differentiation, and it's your strongest empirical result. Without claim labels you can only show it indirectly through decision accuracy.

My read: try for the claim labels, but know you have a defensible fallback if the timeline compresses.

## Claude

Important distinction first: **you're not using DeBERTa off the shelf.** You built a composition — NLI plus entity matching plus negation detection, combined with weights you chose. Published benchmarks justify the *parts*. They say nothing about the *whole*.

So you can't fully outsource this. But there are three routes, and one of them is much cheaper than labeling.

---

**Route 1 — Instrumental validation (free, already in your plan)**

The verifier score is an intermediate variable. Intermediate variables can be validated by their downstream effect.

```
If the composite score produces good decisions
        ↓
the score is doing its job
        ↓
measured via decision accuracy against your
expected_decision labels
```

And critically — **ablation works at the decision level too.** You don't need claim labels for it:

```
NLI only           → decision accuracy X
NLI + entity       → decision accuracy Y
NLI + entity + neg → decision accuracy Z
```

If Z > Y > X, each mechanism earns its place. That answers "which components matter" without a single claim label.

---

**Route 2 — Perturbation-based validation (cheap, and this is the one I'd push)**

This is the move that gets you rigorous verifier validation for a fraction of the labeling cost, and it has clear precedent.

You already have 161 expert-validated gold answers. Perturb them:

```
Original (supported):
"The arm stops within 200ms"
        ↓
Numerical perturbation:
"The arm stops within 500ms"      → label: unsupported

Negation perturbation:
"Lockout is always required"
from "required unless equipment
cannot be locked out"              → label: unsupported

Entity swap:
"Recovery mode" → "Emergency mode" → label: unsupported
```

The labels are **free and unambiguous** — you know they're wrong because you broke them.

The precedent is solid. BUMP (Ma et al., 2023) contributes 889 human-written minimal pairs, each introducing a single error from an ontology of seven types into a reference summary. SummEdits and HaluEval consist of inconsistent summaries corrupted by introducing synthetic factual errors. There's also work explicitly on validating factuality evaluation methods via answer perturbation (arXiv:2609.15561).

Why this is better than generic labeling *for your specific thesis*:

```
Generic claim labels → tests general verifier accuracy
                       where an LLM judge likely wins

Targeted perturbations → tests EXACTLY the failure modes
                        your entity matching and negation
                        detection were built for
                        → where you expect to win
```

You can generate 100+ perturbed pairs in an afternoon, and it directly tests your differentiating claim rather than a general one.

---

**Route 3 — Construct validity (write-up only)**

Each mechanism is motivated by a documented failure mode rather than chosen arbitrarily — entailment models' insensitivity to numerical discrepancy, and to conditional exception language. That's design justification in Chapter 3, not empirical validation, but it belongs in the argument.

---

**What you'd lose without any real labels**

```
Can't say: "my verifier agrees with human
            judgment at X balanced accuracy"

Can say:   "ablation shows each mechanism
            improves decision accuracy"
            and, with perturbations,
            "the hybrid verifier catches 94% of
             numerical corruptions vs 61% for
             NLI alone"
```

That second sentence is actually more persuasive for your thesis than a generic agreement figure.

---

**My recommendation**

```
Do: perturbation set (~100 pairs, one afternoon)
    → balanced accuracy + ROC-AUC on it
    → broken out by perturbation type
Do: decision-level ablation (already planned)
Do: cite component benchmarks

Optional: ~40 naturally-occurring claim labels
    → confirms perturbations aren't unrealistically easy
    → small enough to actually finish
```

The perturbation set is the highest-value thing here. It's cheap, it's established practice, and it measures precisely the thing you claim as your advantage.

Want me to revise the validation section around this — perturbation as primary, natural labels as optional supplement?

**Why there's no shortcut here**

Your verifier is a composition nobody has built — DeBERTa plus entity matching plus negation detection with your weights, on manufacturing safety documents. No published number describes that object, because that object didn't exist before you made it.

That's the cost of having a contribution. If a paper already reported your numbers, you wouldn't have a thesis.

**What SummaC actually is**

SummaC is a verifier. Not yours — theirs.

```
SummaC's job:
Given a document and a summary
        ↓
Is this summary factually consistent
with the document?
        ↓
They built it using NLI models
```

Sound familiar? It's structurally the same problem as yours:

```
SummaC:  document + summary → consistent?
You:     evidence chunk + claim → supported?
```

Different application, same underlying question. That's why their evaluation protocol transfers.

---

**The part you actually use**

Not their verifier. Their **paper's Section 4** — how they proved theirs worked.

```
What they did:
1. Assembled benchmark datasets where
   humans had labeled consistency
2. Ran their verifier on those datasets
3. Reported balanced accuracy (primary)
   and ROC-AUC (secondary)
4. Selected thresholds on a validation set
5. Bootstrap resampling for significance
```

That numbered list is what you copy. Substitute your verifier and your data.

---

**Concretely, what you do**

```
SummaC's version:
Their NLI verifier
    ↓ run on
Their benchmark (human-labeled summaries)
    ↓ report
Balanced accuracy = 0.79 (their number)

Your version:
Your hybrid verifier
(NLI + entity + negation)
    ↓ run on
Your perturbation set (100 pairs,
labels known because you made the errors)
    ↓ report
Balanced accuracy = ??? (your number)
```

Identical procedure. Different verifier, different data, different result.

---

**The two words that matter**

```
Balanced accuracy
→ accuracy that corrects for class imbalance
→ if 80% of your pairs are "supported,"
  plain accuracy is misleading — a verifier
  that says "supported" always scores 80%
→ balanced accuracy averages the accuracy on
  each class separately, so that trick fails

ROC-AUC
→ your verifier outputs a score, not a label
→ AUC asks: if I pick one supported claim and
  one unsupported claim at random, how often
  does the supported one get the higher score?
→ 1.0 = always, 0.5 = coin flip
→ measures ranking quality independent of
  where you set the threshold
```

That second one is quietly important for you. It separates "is my score any good?" from "did I pick a good threshold?" — two different questions Maier may be conflating.

---

**Same structure for the decision layer**

```
SABER's paper:
Swept threshold 0.05 → 0.95
Reported coverage, risk-on-answered,
abstention F1 at each point
        ↓
You do the identical sweep
on your thresholds
with your decision labels
```

---

**What this gets you with Maier**

Right now if he asks "why balanced accuracy?" your answer is "it seemed right." After this, it's:

> Balanced accuracy is the primary metric in SummaC and standard in the factual consistency literature; ROC-AUC is the example-level metric TRUE argues for. I report both, following established practice.

The metric choice stops being yours to defend. Only the numbers are yours.

---

**Concretely, this week**

```
1. Download SummaC (arXiv:2111.09525)
   Read Section 4 only — the evaluation section
   Skip their model architecture entirely

2. Download SABER (arXiv:2605.18792)
   Find the threshold sweep table
   Copy the column headers

3. Build your perturbation set

4. Compute: balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC
   Both are one line in scikit-learn
```

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score, roc_auc_score

balanced_accuracy_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)
roc_auc_score(true_labels, predicted_scores)
```

That's the entire implementation. The hard part was knowing which two functions to call and being able to cite why.

## User

what does pertubation mean?

---

## Claude

**Perturbation** = a small, deliberate change you make to something correct, to see if your system notices.

---

**The everyday version**

```
You want to test a smoke detector
        ↓
You don't wait for a real fire
        ↓
You light a match under it
        ↓
Deliberate, controlled, you know
exactly what you did
        ↓
If it doesn't beep, it's broken
```

Perturbation is lighting the match.

---

**In your case**

You have 161 gold answers that are *correct*. You break them on purpose:

```
Gold answer (correct):
"The arm stops within 200ms"
        ↓
You change ONE thing
        ↓
Perturbed:
"The arm stops within 500ms"
        ↓
You KNOW this is now wrong
because you're the one who changed it
```

Then you feed it to your verifier and see whether it catches it.

---

**Why this solves your labeling problem**

```
Hand-labeling:
Read claim, read evidence, decide
"is this supported?"
→ slow, subjective, needs a second annotator

Perturbation:
You broke it, so you know it's broken
→ fast, objective, zero ambiguity
→ the label comes free with the corruption
```

---

**Your three perturbation types**

Each one targets a mechanism you built:

```
Numerical → tests entity matching
"200ms" → "500ms"
"three modes" → "five modes"

Negation → tests negation detection
Evidence: "required unless X"
Claim:    "always required"

Entity swap → tests entity matching
"Recovery mode" → "Emergency mode"
"1910.147" → "1910.212"
```

---

**And a fourth set you must include**

```
Unperturbed originals
→ left exactly as they are
→ label: supported
```

Without these, your verifier could score 100% by simply saying "unsupported" to everything. You need both classes to measure anything real.

Roughly: 50 unperturbed, 50 perturbed across the three types.

## Claude

Four, in this order. And you don't read any of them cover to cover.

**1. Claim-Selective Certification (arXiv:2605.21949)** — read fully

This one is non-negotiable and urgent. It's your closest prior work, and you need to know exactly what it does before anyone on your committee finds it.

```
Read for:
→ How their pipeline is structured
→ Where they intervene (during vs after generation)
→ How they evaluate
→ Whether it's peer-reviewed or preprint
→ Anything that also covers post-hoc middleware
  (if it does, your framing needs another look)
```

**2. SummaC (arXiv:2111.09525)** — evaluation section only

```
Read for:
→ How they validated their verifier
→ Why balanced accuracy
→ How they picked thresholds
Skip: their model architecture
```

**3. SABER (arXiv:2605.18792)** — the threshold sweep and metrics

```
Read for:
→ How they define coverage and risk
→ The threshold sweep table
→ How they present decision-layer results
Skip: their training method
```

**4. Kernan Freire et al. (arXiv:2401.05200)** — results and discussion

```
Read for:
→ The operator quotes
→ The night-shift scenario
→ Why operators preferred human experts
```

This is your motivation. You'll quote it in Chapter 1 and likely in your defense opening, so you should know it well.

**Hold for later**

TRUE, BUMP, Ji et al., Maynez et al., Megahed's full paper — all useful for Chapter 2, none urgent. You'll cite them; you don't need them to make decisions this month.

what papers should i read for decision layer and metrics...

---

## Claude

Four, split by what each gives you.

---

**For how a decision layer is built and evaluated**

**SABER — "Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach"** (arXiv:2605.18792)

Your closest methodological match. They sweep τ from 0.05 to 0.95 in 0.05 steps and report Score, Coverage, Risk on answered, and abstention F1 at each point.

```
Read: the threshold sweep table and how they
      define each column
Skip: their training approach
```

This is essentially your Experiment 4.4. Copy the table structure.

---

**For the theoretical framing**

**Geifman & El-Yaniv (2017), "Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks"**

The risk-coverage framework itself. Gives you the formal definitions of coverage and selective risk that you'll state in Chapter 5 before reporting numbers.

```
Read: the definitions section only
Skip: the deep learning specifics
```

Cite El-Yaniv & Wiener (2010) alongside it as the origin.

---

**For metric definitions you can cite**

**LIT-RAGBench** (arXiv:2603.06198)

Gives you **over-abstention rate** as a named, published metric — the thing that catches a system refusing when it shouldn't. Directly relevant since "refuses too much" is a real failure mode for you.

---

**For justifying retrieval-based abstention**

**Citation-Enforced RAG** (arXiv:2603.14170)

They ground abstention in retrieval confidence rather than generative uncertainty alone, tying decisions directly to evidence availability.

That's your Retrieval Coverage Check, justified in one sentence you can cite.

---

**Reading order and depth**

```
1. SABER          — 40 min, the sweep table
2. Geifman 2017   — 20 min, definitions only
3. LIT-RAGBench   — 15 min, find the metric
4. Citation-RAG   — 15 min, Section 7.2
```

Under two hours total, and you come out with every metric in your Chapter 5 traceable to a published source.

---

**The four metrics you'll end up reporting**

```
Coverage             → fraction answered
Selective risk       → error rate among answered
Over-abstention rate → refused despite being answerable
Abstention F1        → overall decision quality
```

Each one now has a citation behind it. That's what Maier was asking for.

Short answer: you don't export the chat, and you wouldn't want to. Let me explain why, then give you the right mechanism.

**Why the raw chat is the wrong thing to give Claude Code**

This conversation is 100+ turns, and most of it is deliberation that got overturned — the OSHA dataset plan, DesignQA, the four-hallucination-types framing I got wrong, the LLM-judge hybrid we rejected, the whole-answer NLI discussion. Dumping that in would have Claude Code re-suggesting things you already ruled out.

**The right mechanism: CLAUDE.md**

CLAUDE.md files are loaded into the context window at the start of every session, and the file becomes part of Claude's system prompt, so every conversation starts with this context already loaded.

The recommendation is to keep this file concise and human-readable, treating it like documentation that both humans and Claude need to understand quickly.

It also supports imports — CLAUDE.md files support importing additional files using `@path/to/import` syntax. So your structure becomes:

```
rag-trust-layer/
├── CLAUDE.md              ← auto-loaded every session
│                            short; points to the others
├── CONTEXT.md             ← architecture, dataset, stack
├── EVALUATION_PLAN.md     ← experiments, validation
└── src/
```

`CLAUDE.md` stays short because it consumes context at every session start. The detailed files get pulled in on demand or via `@` reference.

**What's missing from your current files**

One thing: a record of what you *rejected* and why. Without it, Claude Code will helpfully suggest LLM-as-judge, or OSHA-only datasets, or whole-answer verification — all paths you closed deliberately.

Want me to write the `CLAUDE.md` plus a short `DECISIONS.md` capturing the rejected paths? That's the actual export of this conversation — the decisions, not the transcript.

Good news — the official export exists, and your instinct to keep everything in one place is right. You just need both layers, not one.

**Getting the transcript out**

Individual Claude users can export chat history from Settings > Privacy on the web app or Claude Desktop (not possible from iOS or Android).

The steps: click your initials in the lower left corner, select Settings, navigate to the Privacy section, click Export data. Once processed, you receive a download link via email.

Two things to know: it exports your **entire account**, not this one chat, and it arrives as JSON rather than a readable transcript. The link expires in about 24 hours, so download promptly.

**The structure you want**

```
rag-trust-layer/
├── CLAUDE.md              ← auto-loaded EVERY session
│                            keep short — it costs tokens
├── CONTEXT.md             ← architecture, dataset, stack
├── EVALUATION_PLAN.md     ← experiments, validation
└── docs/
    └── thesis-chat.md     ← full transcript
                             reference only, NOT auto-loaded
```

The critical rule: CLAUDE.md files are loaded into the context window at the start of every session, consuming tokens alongside your conversation. A 100+ turn transcript would eat your context before you type anything.

So the transcript lives in the repo — searchable, greppable, and you can point Claude Code at a specific section when you need it (*"read docs/thesis-chat.md lines 2000-2200"*) — but it never auto-loads.

**Want me to write the conversion script now?** The export gives you JSON with every conversation in your account. A small Python script can pull out just this thesis thread and write it as clean markdown. I can write it today so it's ready when the email arrives — you'd just point it at the ZIP.

No dependencies beyond the standard library.

**Two things worth knowing**

The script tries several key names for every field — `sender`/`role`, `text`/`content`, `chat_messages`/`messages` — because the export schema has changed across versions. If Anthropic changes it again, it degrades to "(untitled)" rather than crashing.

And the ambiguity guard matters for you specifically: you'll likely have several conversations with "thesis" in the title. Searching by title stops and lists them rather than guessing, which is why you go UUID-first.

**Add to `.gitignore` before you unzip anything:**

```
*.zip
conversations.json
```

The export contains your entire account, not just this thread. You want the one extracted markdown file in the repo, not the raw dump.

## Claude

Four steps. The first one has to happen before anything else.

**Step 1 — Request the export**

```
claude.ai → click your initials (bottom left)
→ Settings
→ Privacy
→ Export data
```

You'll get an email with a download link. **The link expires in about 24 hours**, so watch for it. This has to be done on web or desktop — not the mobile app.

**Step 2 — Download the ZIP**

Put it somewhere outside your repo, like `~/Downloads`. Don't unzip it — the script reads the ZIP directly.

**Step 3 — Find this conversation**

```bash
cd ~/path/to/rag-trust-layer
python extract_chat.py ~/Downloads/data-export.zip --list --search thesis
```

You'll get a table like:

```
DATE          TURNS  UUID                    TITLE
2026-01-15      247  a1b2c3d4-...            Thesis topic selection
2026-02-03       12  e5f6g7h8-...            Thesis writing help
```

**This conversation will have by far the most turns** — that's how you identify it. Copy its UUID.

**Step 4 — Extract**

```bash
python extract_chat.py ~/Downloads/data-export.zip \
    --uuid a1b2c3d4-... \
    -o docs/thesis-chat.md
```

The export is your entire Claude account. You want the one extracted markdown file in your repo — not the raw dump.

## Claude

Yes — VS Code's terminal is exactly the right place.

```
1. Open VS Code
2. Open your rag-trust-layer folder
3. Open the terminal (Ctrl + ` or View → Terminal)
4. Activate your venv:
   source venv/bin/activate
5. Run the commands
```

Two things to get right:

**Put `extract_chat.py` in your project root** — same level as `CONTEXT.md`. Then the commands work exactly as written.

**Use the full path to the ZIP.** The ZIP lives in Downloads, your terminal is in the project folder. So:

```bash
python extract_chat.py ~/Downloads/data-export.zip --list --search thesis
```

The `~/Downloads/` part matters — without it Python looks in your project folder and won't find the file.

---

If you'd rather not type the path, drag the ZIP file from Finder into the VS Code terminal. It pastes the full path automatically.
